items.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
items.content:
Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432, a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 . The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10, and , and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel, and as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release, and Red Hat lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix.

the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. See the timeline.

CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA
Critical, CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat rates it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1 (), SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1.
Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE)
Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat: "primarily results in a system crash leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential memory corruption."
7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18)
Ubuntu (every release), RHEL 8, 9, and 10, Amazon Linux 2, and Amazon Linux 2023's default kernel, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix.
Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit.
Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29.
Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit.

Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue."

Distribution kernels carry backported fixes under their own version numbers, so check the tracker, not the upstream number. As of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29:

  • the tracker lists the package as "Vulnerable" on every release. On 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 it adds "work in progress" in , , , and ; 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable." Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published.
  • RHEL 8, 9, and 10 and OpenShift Container Platform 4 are listed as affected, with no fix; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected (CVE page). Red Hat says mitigation "is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria."
  • fixed in 12 "bookworm" (, DLA-4841-1, and , DLA-4850-1), 13 "trixie" (, DSA-6568-1), and unstable (tracker).
  • rated important. SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 () and the 15 SP4, SP5, and SP6 LTSS kernels are fixed; 15 SP7 is in progress, and openSUSE Leap 15.6 and 16.0 are listed as affected (CVE page).
  • rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK) errata for Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10 came out October 16: ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, and ELSA-2026-500399 (CVE page). The page lists only the UEK kernels.
  • rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. On Amazon Linux 2023, is fixed (ALAS2023-2026-3251, October 24) and is fixed (ALAS2023-2026-3335, October 29). The default package and every Amazon Linux 2 kernel are "Pending Fix" (CVE page).

#How the vulnerability works

When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection, the kernel tracks the half-open handshake in a lightweight "request socket," then creates a full socket once the handshake completes. If the connecting peer's IPv4 header carried options, the kernel keeps them to echo in its replies. The bug: the kernel handed those saved options from the request socket to the new connection without copying them, then freed them immediately when the connection went away, while another CPU could still be reading them to build a handshake reply. Reading freed kernel memory is a use-after-free.

The peer needs no login, and it all happens inside the kernel's handshake handling, before any application code runs. The CNA's scoring notes say the stale data can leak kernel heap memory back to the peer, steer kernel writes out of bounds, or crash the machine. Anthropic says a lost race "only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed."

Eric Dumazet's commit, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," changes two plain calls to , which waits until every reader has finished with the memory before freeing it. Other code paths that replace these options already did that. The commit also fixes the same problem in request-socket migration (net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program), and says a related IPv6 case "will be addressed in a separate patch."

#Which servers are exposed

  • Every Linux host that accepts IPv4 TCP connections on an affected kernel: web servers, SSH, databases, load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes. The CNA's notes say the vulnerable path runs "during the TCP handshake, before application authentication."
  • Hosts with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener first. That's the setup Anthropic's working exploit needs: "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Anthropic hasn't said why that listener matters, and the CVE record doesn't mention MPTCP. A server has one only if an application opens an MPTCP socket; the check is below.

Red Hat rates the bug lower than the CNA. It scores the attack complexity as High (CVSS 8.1) and describes the result as mainly a crash "or potential memory corruption." Anthropic's lab exploit shows a remote root shell on at least one configuration, so a lower rating isn't a reason to wait.

#How to check your systems

Compare the result with your distribution's status above, not with the upstream version. If the installed kernel is newer than the running one, the fix isn't active until you reboot. Run these on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes, not inside containers: a container reports the host's kernel. We ran them on a Debian 12 host and in a Rocky Linux 9 container.

#Check for multipath TCP listeners

lists only MPTCP sockets, so an empty result means no MPTCP listener. alone doesn't create one: an application has to open an MPTCP socket. We tested both with iproute2 6.1 in a Debian 12 container, where listed a test MPTCP listener and skipped a plain TCP one beside it.

#Update the kernel and reboot

Install your distribution's fixed kernel as soon as it ships, then reboot: a kernel update doesn't take effect until the machine boots into it. Reboot container hosts and Kubernetes nodes too. Appliances and cloud images that bundle a kernel need their vendor's update.

On Debian, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and the 15 LTSS releases, Oracle Linux's UEK kernels, and Amazon Linux 2023's and , the fix is out. On Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux 2, and Amazon Linux 2023's default kernel, it isn't yet, as of 8:00 PM CDT, October 29. Watch the trackers linked above. Running a self-built kernel? Move to the fixed stable release for its line.

Red Hat publishes no mitigation. The following is Atlas's interim recommendation, based on the CNA's scoring notes, which say the attacking peer supplies IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options in its SYN. TCP traffic almost never carries IPv4 options legitimately, so dropping TCP packets that have them should cost nothing:

matches any IPv4 header longer than the 20-byte minimum, which only options produce. The rule runs before connection tracking and doesn't touch IPv6 or non-TCP traffic. We tested it in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a SYN carrying a Record Route option, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. We haven't tested it against an exploit, and it doesn't fix the kernel. It lasts until reboot, which is fine if the reboot is into a fixed kernel; remove it with nft delete table ip cve_2026_98432. If your edge firewall can drop IPv4 packets with options, doing it there protects every host behind it.

Until then, keep MPTCP listeners off the internet, and put the hosts that have one at the top of the patch list.

#Timeline and exploitation status

All times are CDT (UTC−5).

Eric Dumazet posts the fix, crediting Xinyang Ge of Anthropic as reporter
The fix is merged into the kernel's networking tree
Linux 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 ship the fix; 7.3-rc7 follows that night
Linux 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 ship the fix; the CVE record is published at 7:08 AM
Oracle publishes UEK errata with the fix for Oracle Linux 7 through 10
Linux 7.3 is released with the fix
Amazon Linux 2023's package is fixed
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team describes a remote root exploit for the bug, built by Claude in its lab
Ubuntu still lists its kernels as vulnerable; Amazon Linux 2023's package is fixed; GitHub repositories referencing the CVE appear, one created at 7:22 PM describing a race trigger

Anthropic says Claude wrote the exploit "after initial prompting," that it runs "arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction" on servers with a multipath TCP listener, and that in its proof of concept "it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." Anthropic hasn't published the exploit. Its disclosure policy gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before Anthropic discusses details beyond a public advisory. By 8:00 PM CDT on October 29, eight GitHub repositories referenced the CVE. Most describe themselves as audit or mitigation tooling, among them an Ansible role and a livepatch for AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux. One, created at 7:22 PM, says it includes a race trigger. The CVE isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of 8:00 PM CDT. We haven't tested any public proof of concept, and we aren't linking them.

We'll revise this post and mark it updated when any of these change: fixed kernels from Ubuntu, Red Hat, or Amazon Linux; NVD's analysis; a KEV listing or any report of exploitation; the separate IPv6 fix.

  • Added Oracle Linux, fixed in its UEK kernels since October 16, and Amazon Linux, fixed in Amazon Linux 2023's 6.12 and 6.18 kernels and pending elsewhere. Eight GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, one describing a race trigger. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, NVD, and KEV are unchanged since 11:00 AM, and nothing was corrected.

items.title: The Duty of a Scholar
items.content:
On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.

There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.

This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.

Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.

In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.

Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done . As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.

Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.

In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:

The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!

The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.

Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.

Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.

This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.

In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.

It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar.

items.title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode
items.content:
I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:

A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube.

Similar to my previous post, this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).

Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:

Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:

I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.

The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.

Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.

I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.

I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!

items.title: It's the Memory Latency, Stupid
items.content:
When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%?

The answer is usually .

Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every memory access from RAM.

Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering.

Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses.

To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity:

(
    &,
    batch: ,
    _sender: &<>,
) -> unary::<()> {
     group_keys = batch.(.key_column).::<>();
     &key  group_keys.() {
        
        *.counts.(key).() += ;
    }
}

We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per , meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per - I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique . Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores.

 > config.yaml <<:
  : 127.0.0.1:5440
: 1
:
  :
    : pivotlake
    : ./data
    : true
:
  :
    :
      : trust
 3  server  config.yaml &
 7  127.0.0.1  5440  pivot

This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache.

You'll notice we did . This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op:

 stat  3  backend_bound_memory,retiring --  7  127.0.0.1  5440  pivot 
Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        8364109137      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     50.1 %  backend_bound_memory
       38233214040      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        8977647849      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       11861387798      ls_not_halted_cyc
       11431618219      ex_ret_ops                       #     16.1 %  retiring
       11858248045      ls_not_halted_cyc

       4.030148989 seconds time elapsed

This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations.

Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches):

 stat  3    ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   --  7  127.0.0.1  5440  pivot 
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          76190837      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.996301634 seconds time elapsed

Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching).

Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases:

In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096).

(
    &,
    batch: ,
    _sender: &<>,
) -> unary::<()> {
     keys = batch.(.key_column).::<>();
     &key  keys.() {
         hash = .hasher.(key);
         partition = (hash >> )  usize;
        .partitions[partition].(&.allocator, (hash, key));
    }
    (())
}

When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1.

() -> unary::<<::>> {
     groups = ::();
     rows  &.partitions {
         table: <(u64, i64, u64)> = ::();   
        rows.(|(hash, key)| {
             table.(hash, |group| group. == key, |group| group.) {
                ::( group) => group.(). += ,
                ::(slot) => { slot.((hash, key, )); }
            }
        });
        groups.(table.().(|(_, key, count)| (key, count)));
    }
    ((::(groups)))
}

At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs.

The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps . By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it!

 7  127.0.0.1  5440  pivot

And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again:

You may notice we're actually doing work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. items.title: I post trained a model on Demoscenes
items.content:
Lately, I have been fascinated by the world of demoscening and sizecoding and eventually I came across HellMood’s remarkable MS DOS demo Whilst reading through his writeup, I became interested in the author had at some of its visual effects. I was struggling to create any of my own, so I hoped to squeeze out a little bit of inspiration out of that.

I noticed that these effects could be traced back to earlier experiments consisting of alternative implementations and several ideas borrowed from previous demos. I began wondering how many other directions the same underlying ideas might have taken. I decided to start with a few existing demos, the simplest ones of all, and modify them character by character to observe how those changes can affect the visual feel.

I came across Dwitter.net, which is like Twitter but for 140 character JavaScript demos. They already supported “remix”-ing any so that we can build on top of them. Co incidentally, the most liked Dweet on the site shared the same effect as the parallax checkerboard effect from !

Digging a little deeper, I noticed some remixes shared substantial portions of their source code, differing by only a few characters, whilst others achieved similar visual effects through entirely different implementations.

Here is an example, I traced back d/36555 from d/367547 which in turn is derived from d/36467. The gray underlined substrings show what is common across all of them. Blue shows what’s common in between the first two, and green shows for the next couple.

In linguistics, language is productive i.e. a finite vocabulary and a finite set of grammatical rules permit an number of different expressions. Programming languages share this property too. Now let’s consider the aforementioned Dweets. They contain overlapping substrings, but their rendered results differ. Suppose you take a 140 character program, and remove its final 30 characters. Even with a hypothetical alphabet of just 64 character, there are almost 1.5 x 10^54 possible completion strings that can be formed. Almost all will be syntactically invalid or produce uninteresting results. Nevertheless, the number of possibilities is astronomical.

It’s not humanly possible to enumerate all of them exhaustively and it would be foolish to to generate and test all possible strings. However, the continuations of a partial program are not equally plausible.

Given a partial program, certain characters and expressions are considerably more likely to follow than others. This is pretty much how autoregressive language models work. I wondered whether I could use such a model to sample plausible continuations of unfinished Dweets and visualize the different directions each program could have taken.

And then, I could surgically delete substrings or mix-and-match them to my own aesthetic taste.

I had also grown rather frustrated with my own ability to “finish” a demo after starting one, so having an autocomplete that understood the peculiar language of Dweeting rather looked like an appealing prospect to me.

That gave me another excuse to experiment - could I inject own aesthetic taste as a prior into my autocomplete model? That’d be really amazing.

I understand that no one can write a function that determines whether a demo is beautiful, but people their preferences by comparing examples, right?

With that in mind, I decided to put my GitHub Sponsors payout towards renting a GPU and post training a model of my own.

The first hurdle was finding a suitable dataset. I initially experimented with generating synthetic Dweets using Claude Sonnet 5.5 but found them not at all aesthetically pleasant. Fortunately, Dwitter.net provides an API, which I used to build a modest dataset of 25k Dweets to be used for training along with ~1.3k more as a validation set.

I used Qwen2.5-Code-7B as the base model. It struggled to complete most of the Dweets I tested it on, which was understandable given how peculiar their syntax is. Dweets make extensive use of code golfing tricks and mathematical shorthand, which are rather unusual compared with the code a general purpose coding model typically encounters.

I decided to try continued pretraining (CPT) on the corpus, hoping to shift the model’s probability distribution towards the pecular language of dweeting. To see whether it had worked, I measured the of individual tokens before and after training. Surprisal is simply the negative log probability a model assigns to a token given everything preceding it. The less likely a token is, the more surprising it is to the model.

In the figure below, darker red indicates greater surprisal. After CPT, much of the code becomes noticeably less surprising (particularly the unfamiliar programming idioms).

Across 30 held out dweets, perplexity fell from 28.63 to 8.57, which means that the model had become substantially better at predicting the structure of these tiny weird programs.

Although the generated programs were more consistent, they still lacked a certain “charm”. Fortunately, Dwitter has an “awesomeness” score for every Dweet. I decided to use it to construct a curriculum.

I ranked the top 5k dweets by their “awesomeness” scores and constructed a curriculum that gradually favoured the more appreciated programs. Initially, every dweet had an equal probability of being sampled. Over 400 training steps, I progressively increased the weight assigned to higher ranked programs, until the top 1000 accounted for roughly 67% of the sampling probability.

This turned out to be a breakthrough! The generated continuations became much more visually interesting.

Interestingly, the improvements in token likelihood extended even to Dweets that had never been sampled during curriculum training. Perplexity fell from 7.42 to 5.65, although the gains were spread fairly evenly across awesomeness ranks.

Across 7000 Dweets, curriculum training improved token likelihood across all awesomeness ranks, including programs never sampled during training. The gains were particularly pronounced for programs the original model found difficult.

I now had a model that could produce rather beautiful continuations. I wondered whether I could take this further by incorporating my own aesthetic preferences.

In mid-September, I came across Surya’s article on Training AI to Paint with Code, where they had used RL to produce watercolor paintings using p5js. They experimented with different reward functions before settling on pairwise comparsions against a collection of hand rated paintings. I remembered that idea and thought of trying something similar with Demoscener (it doesn’t feel alright to call it “the model” repeatedly).

I opted to do RLHF using GRPO, with myself acting as the reward function.

For each unfinished Dweet, I sampled a group of eight completions, rendered them side by side and selected the one I found most aesthetically pleasing. If none appealed to me, I skipped the group. I used these preferences to update Demoscener’s policy, then sampled fresh continuations and repeated the process over roughly 9–10 rounds of 500 groups each. Altogether, I manually inspected around 40,000 animations.

Somewhere around the 10,000th animation, I began to appreciate the existence of VLMs and HPSv3. Sadly, it was too late.

After several rounds of training, I wanted to see how much of my taste had actually rubbed off on Demoscener. I enlisted a rather unwilling friend to judge 400 sets of demos from a few of the checkpoints (I picked 4 randomly), without knowing which model had produced which.

The results showed that checkpoint 4 was the most favorable, so I used that to run inference on my Mac.

Now coming to the end of the side quest, I built a little interface where I could generate several continuations from the same prefix, render them side by side and branch off from whichever one caught my eye. I could then tweak the code, generate more continuations, and keep exploring.

Each branch represents a possible continuation, which I could compare visually, tweak by hand, and use as the starting point for further exploration.

There is something quite lovely about being able to wander through these possibilities. I think I'll be spending a little more time doing just that.

William Nordhaus has died
items.content:
Nordhaus began contemplating the economics of climate change in the 1970s, when few economists — or anyone else — were thinking about or studying it. The model that he developed — together with his dozens of articles, worldwide lectures, and numerous books — paved the way for a vast body of research which continues to frame the ongoing debate on how best to address the threat of climate change.

Along the way, Nordhaus served his field and the nation: as an editor of scientific journals, a member of the Congressional Budget Office Panel of Economic Experts, the first chairman of the Advisory Committee for the Bureau of Economic Analysis, a chairman of the Board of Directors of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, and as a member of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers. He was a member of the National Academy of Sciences and a distinguished fellow and president of the American Economic Association.

Not to be ignored among his extraordinary accomplishments is his co-authorship of multiple edits of the textbook “Economics.” The textbook, first published in 1948 by economist Paul Samuelson, the first American to win the Nobel Prize in economics, remains the standard-bearer for the principles of economics courses nationwide. Nordhaus became co-author in 1985 and continued as the primary author, revising and updating it after Samuelson’s 2009 death, and maintaining it through its most recent 19th edition. In recent years he was working on a project through Lighthouse Books to make an economics textbook freely available to all learners. 

William Nordhaus was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, where his family gained prominence for its many civic contributions. His father, a Yale College and Yale Law School graduate, made his law firm one of the nation’s most prominent advocates of Indian law, focusing on the representation of American Indian tribes, tribal corporations, and Native American organizations; in 1984 his firm won a landmark water case for the Jicarilla Apache Nation. He also pioneered skiing in New Mexico’s Sandia Mountains and founded what became the Sandia Peak Ski Area, located in the Cibola National Forest. The younger Nordhaus remained a skier all his life.

Nordhaus arrived at Yale as an undergraduate in 1959, an event that he called “one of the great windfalls of my life”; he described Yale as a “paradise for minds coming to the age of abstract reason.” He took Directed Studies (), an intensive program for first-year students, and was taught by professors Vincent Scully, Leonard Krieger, Victor Brombert, and Richard Bernstein. These scholar-teachers, Nordhaus would say, “were role models for his future academic life.” He went on to graduate school at , another place he thought of as a kind of paradise – he called it “Arcadia.” He was mentored there by Nobel laureates Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow, and his class was filled with young economists who would also become leaders of their generation.  

Hired as an assistant professor at Yale right after completing graduate school, Nordhaus from the start on was involved in university affairs. The opposite of an insular scholar, he was an important figure in his department and on campus, teaching undergraduates as well as graduate students and appearing regularly at Connecticut Hall faculty meetings. When a Faculty of Arts and Sciences faculty senate was established, in 2015, he was one of its inaugural members and later its chair.

items.content:
Telegram channel called ‘Leakers$’

incident

circulated on social media

statement Thursday evening

The ministry did not identify the international company, the countries affected, or any suspects. It also gave no technical explanation of how the alleged website breach translated into control over roadside advertising displays.

The group’s account broadly supports the ministry’s description of an international incident but provides a different level of technical detail.

“It was a genuine vulnerability in the software responsible for transmitting content to LED displays,” the person said. “After exploiting it, we gained access to display systems in several countries, not just Egypt, but also Malaysia, Brazil, China, and others.”

The person added that the infrastructure was not exclusive to Egypt and contained multiple security flaws, including weaknesses accessible through the system’s own pages and interfaces.

Asked whether the operation involved exploiting an unknown software vulnerability or merely accessing poorly protected equipment exposed to the public internet, the representative described a software flaw but did not provide enough technical evidence to establish the precise method.

According to the representative, the group located its targets through automated scanning rather than selecting particular companies or countries.

“The systems were identified through an automated and random scan,” they said, adding that several participants using the online pseudonyms Never, 19ylegal, CH and Nivex were involved in identifying thousands of exposed systems over approximately two hours.

The representative shared visual records captured during the incident and referred to material on the group’s public Telegram channel.

In its initial public statement, the group said its objective was to expose security failures rather than demand payment or carry out a ransomware attack.

“Companies charge millions to build infrastructure across multiple countries and leave LED screens and billboard networks wide open on the internet without basic protection,” the statement said.

The group also rejected the idea that taking control of the screens required advanced technical capabilities.

Perhaps most importantly, the intrusion raises questions about cybersecurity oversight at Arabian United, whose shareholders include one of the Egyptian state’s most politically influential media companies.

UMS, the media arm of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service, was established in 2016 and controls more than 40 companies across television, newspapers, digital media, entertainment, and advertising.

The billboard’s operator, Arabian United, however, was established in 2022 through a partnership between UMS and Arabian Contracting Services Co., one of Saudi Arabia’s largest outdoor advertising businesses.

2025 annual report

March 2026 financial statements

The company’s annual report also says it supervises, manages, and operates every stage of the advertising process in Egypt, from installing screens and securing advertising clients to displaying their content.

That division of responsibilities is significant because the Interior Ministry attributed the incident to an “international service provider” without identifying it or explaining its contractual relationship with the Egyptian operator.

When asked what the incident suggested about the security capabilities of an advertising business associated with Egyptian intelligence, the group’s representative said such institutional connections offered no guarantee against technical weaknesses.

“If infrastructure operated by a company linked to Egyptian intelligence can be compromised, it demonstrates that such connections do not necessarily translate into strong cybersecurity,” the representative said.

Obviously, the association with UMS does not establish that Egyptian intelligence agencies were responsible for administering the compromised systems. It does, however, place the incident within a security apparatus-linked commercial network that has expanded its presence across some of Egypt’s most heavily monitored public spaces.

acknowledged the intrusion

The company said it had immediately suspended the screen, was investigating the incident in coordination with authorities, and that it “remained committed to the highest security and operating standards.”

told

The incident also exposes a gap between the government’s extensive regulation of roadside advertising content and the publicly disclosed safeguards governing the digital systems on which that advertising increasingly depends.

Law No. 208 of 2020

The authority is responsible for setting standards governing roadside advertising, including requirements concerning “public order and morality.”

September 2025 meeting

Neither that regulatory framework nor the government’s latest statements explain what cybersecurity standards apply to remotely operated advertising networks, whether the affected operator had undergone a security assessment, or who bears responsibility for auditing third-party software connected to publicly visible screens.

The Interior Ministry said legal procedures had been initiated but did not specify whether the investigation would examine failures by the Egyptian operator or its contractors.

items.title: Copyright Office is restoring copyright to something you have to work to get
items.content:
• Formalities: When it comes to AI, the Copyright Office is restoring copyright to its proper status, as something you have to work to get.
  • Object permanence: GWB x martial law; Li'l Sparky; Dueling Starbuckses; Microsoft buys Skype (does fuckery); Bieber v SOPA; SOPA is the worst; Snowden x rule of law; "Laserwriter II"; Russia v DST; Class war funnies; Minnesota's miracle; Icelandic women v sexism; Image analogies; Aussie DMCA ratfucked; "Authorised Domain"; Sales tax is regressive; Prince Charles's secret veto; Wells Fargo blackballed workers for refusing to crime; Poe read by Vincent Price and Basil Rathbone; Put it back!; The internet was made for privacy.
  • Upcoming appearances: Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal.

It's not often that I find myself on the same side as the US Copyright Office. In fact, I think this is the first time in 25 years that I've found myself cheering on the office's official actions as good for art good for free expression, taking the side of creative workers over our bosses.

The source of our miraculous accord: the US Copyright Office's position on AI. The CO has taken the (entirely correct) position that copyright law exists to incentivize human acts of creative expression, which means that only works of human authorship are eligible for copyright.

This isn't a controversial position within legal circles. But for media executives, this is shocking; absurd, even. This gap between the industrial and the legal understanding of copyright comes from a fundamental difference over the evocatively named legal doctrine of "sweat of the brow."

"Sweat of the brow" is fundamental to a correct legal understanding of copyright. Copyright rewards and protects but it does protect . You can labor for ten years over a phone book listing the numbers of every person in a town and (as a collection of uncopyrightable facts) it will receive protection . Zero. Zilch. Anyone can copy and sell that phone book:

Copyright law doesn't care if you slaved over that collection of facts, if you missed sleep and your kids' little league games to realize your grand vision. Copyright law doesn't care if you plowed every cent into it, remortgaging your home and cashing in your (already resentful) kids' college funds.

But: if you dash off a haiku in ten seconds while sitting on the toilet, shove it into your pocket and forget about it, and then your (still resentful) kids discover that crumpled haiku after your (highly suspicious) death, your kids will be able to claim a full worth of copyright over that forgotten triviality (the term of copyright for works of human authorship is life plus 70 years).

This is the uncontroversial and universally accepted understanding of copyright: all the copyright in the world for creative acts, no copyright at all for mere acts of labor. The "sweat of the brow" has nothing to do with a work's eligibility for copyright.

But no media boss believes this. For media bosses, copyright is a pseudo-property† right, designed and operated to protect their bottom line. The point of copyright isn't to incentivize , but rather .

There's obviously a relationship between creative acts and acts of investment, but it's possible to create without investment (see: your haiku) and it's possible to invest without creativity (see: your phone book).

And once again, the creativity that copyright protects is creativity. This is a lesson that David Slater learned the hard way. Slater is a professional wildlife photographer and amateur monkey-trainer who combined his interests by teaching Celebes crested macaque monkeys to take selfies. But when Slater published a monkey's selfie others copied and distributed the image without his permission, on the (entirely legally correct) basis that monkeys are not humans, and that means that works created by monkeys don't get a copyright. This was also the Copyright Office's position, and the position of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals:

This is the basis for the US Copyright Office's repeated decision to refuse to extend copyright to AI-generated works. An algorithm is even human than a monkey, so if you can't get copyright over a monkey selfie, you can't copyright your chatbot's slop. The US Copyright Office has successfully defended this position in multiple courts, triumphing over plaintiffs who were so persistent that they even got the Supreme Court to weigh in on the issue (the Supremes decided the case didn't warrant their attention):

AI slop isn't copyrightable, but there can be copyrightable in an AI-generated image. The most obvious element is the prompt. So long as your prompt contains some quantum of creativity (e.g. "Make me a beautiful flower whose loveliness is reminiscent of a newborn baby", but not "make me a beautiful flower"), that prompt copyrightable. That means you can use copyright to challenge others' rights to present the same prompt to a chatbot. But while the prompt can be copyrighted, the image it gives rise to . So you can spend a month iteratively refining your prompt, consuming all your town's water along with 200,000 gallons of diesel and that prompt will be yours for your life plus 70 years, but the image it generates is in the public domain, and anyone can copy it, sell it or give it away.

There are other ways that copyright can find its way into AI-generated material. You can make creative edits to it: if you output a slop novel and rewrite various sentences (providing those rewrites involve some creativity and not just mechanical corrections or word substitutions), then the edited sentences become copyrighted works, even though all the rest of the text remains uncopyrightable.

You can also get a "thin" copyright through selection. If you get your chatbot to output images based on your prompt and choose your favorite, your selection can confer a bit of copyright over that creative act of selection, but it will be harder to defend than even the other (attenuated and highly specific) forms of copyright.

Now, perhaps you've spotted an administrative problem lurking in this turn of events. How can someone else know what part of a work is AI-generated (and thus in the public domain) and which parts are human-edited/contributed (and thus copyrighted)? Just as importantly, how can prove which parts of your work are not AI-generated and thus eligible for copyright protection.

This gets especially gnarly when you're dealing with complex media. In an animation, an AI might do the rigging and movement for a human-created sprite. The sprite is copyrightable, but its movements aren't. That would mean that I could remap your sprite's movements onto a different sprite without infringing your copyright. Or say the sprite and its movements are human created (and thus copyrighted), but the backgrounds are procedurally generated? I could take those backgrounds and put new animations overtop of them.

The simplest, most reliable way to ensure the works you invest in are fully and entirely eligible for copyright is to just use humans for the whole project. Declare a "no-AI policy," and hire human artists to produce the works you hope to sell. Monitor their activity to ensure they're not using AI. Keep good records.

Now, as much as I like the idea that we've arrived at a copyright law that insists that a company can only get exclusive rights to its products by paying human artists to make them from end-to-end, I don't think that's likely to be the way it shakes out, but that doesn't mean that this is a wash for artists.

The reality is that copyright claims are "fact-intensive inquiries" that are expensive to litigate and difficult to adjudicate. It's completely for copyright lawsuits to turn on documentary evidence gleaned from fragmentary records. This is simply intrinsic to copyright, because copyright is a doctrine that requires judges to assess whether things are "creative" and "original" as though these were freestanding categories that everyone could agree upon.

Of course, the rules of copyright can make this harder or easier. One way in which the rules make deciding copyright cases is copyright's broad prohibition on "formalities" ("formalities" is how copyright wonks refer to "red tape" or "paperwork"). For nearly all of American history, copyright ran on a key formality: deposit, registration and notice.

To secure a copyright for a new work, an artist (or their employer) had to send a copy of that work to the Library of Congress (deposit), along with paperwork detailing the claim of authorship (who made this, what parts of it did they make) (registration) and they had to display a copyright that told you who held the copyright to every work that was registered (notice). Both the filing and the notice required careful attention and precision, and screwing either one up could result in your losing your copyright. It's an open secret among copyright scholars that Walt Disney screwed this up with the first Mickey cartoons, meaning they've been in the public domain since their release:

This system of copyright formalities meant that you could always tell whether a work was copyrighted, you could always find out who claimed the copyright over it, and which parts of the work were claimed under copyright and under what basis. What's more, formalities created the Library of Congress, since the LoC acted as America's "copyright deposit" library, holding deposit copies of every work that had ever been issued a US copyright.

The US system of formalities was descended from the English system, in which the Stationers' Guild used a copyright registry to establish who had the rights to which books. But there were competing copyright systems, notably the "continental" system that was codified through the Berne Convention, a copyright treaty drafted by Victor Hugo (yes, Victor Hugo).

Among other things, the Berne Convention abolished formalities. Much of the world adopted Berne, but the US held out until 1976. With the 1976 Copyright Act, Congress brought the US into compliance with Berne, abolishing formalities in the USA. As a compromise, the 1976 Act requires US authors to register their copyrights in order to obtain "statutory damages" (up to $150,000 per work). That's a pretty good incentive, but even with that incentive, the vast majority – far in excess of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999% – of all copyrighted works are not registered with the Copyright Office. They are born copyrighted from the moment they are "fixed in a tangible medium" until 70 years after their authors die. But without registration, you can't know when that copyright clock started ticking because you have no way to verify who the author of the work is. This not only makes it difficult to establish the copyright status of nearly every copyrighted work, but it also means that in nearly every case, you can't readily determine who you should approach if you want to pay them for a copyright license.

Abolishing formalities has created a universe of orphan works: everything from napkin doodles to kindergartners' finger paintings to message board posts. Within that universe is a kind of gaseous cloud that, if condensed, would come out to an infinitesimal planetoid, representing the entirety of commercial works whose authors give a damn about their copyright status. It's a bad, bad system.

This system doesn't do away with the need to keep careful records: like I said, copyright disputes usually require the close examination of documentary evidence. What formality abolition accomplished was the destruction of the regular system of record-keeping: rather than having a standard, universally agreed-upon way to determine the status and resolve disputes about a copyrighted work, now we have the scattershot, incoherent system that makes copyright disputes more likely (because no one knows who to approach for copyright licenses) far more difficult to resolve (because there's no registry of copyrighted works).

Which brings me back to the question of AI and copyright. If a firm uses AI in its work, it's going to need to document that carefully. Firms that don't keep very close track of the elements of their products that come from AI will have a far harder time defending their commercial interests.

Basically, we're about to recreate formalities, but managed by the private sector. To the extent that companies use AI in their work, they are going to have to track every pixel and every word and every note that is output by an AI system, and which parts were added or edited by humans after creation.

That means that companies that want to protect their commercial interests aren't just going to get more protection based on how much work they get humans to do; they're also going to have to treat copyright's government-enforceable monopoly over expressive speech with the gravitas it deserves: not something you get automatically, but something you have to do real administrative work for.

items.title: What is a light-day? The milestone Voyager 1 is closing in on
items.content:
The milestone Voyager 1 is closing in on is about distance, not time. And it's very, very far.

The Voyager 1 spacecraft, traveling for nearly 50 years, will soon cross a mile marker reached by no other human-made object — one light-day away from Earth. That’s the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equaling about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), a point that Voyager 1 will reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST.

Voyager 1 to Reach One Light-Day

Its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, took a different path through the solar system after they launched in 1977, in order to visit Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is on pace to be one light-day away from Earth in nine more years, in November 2035.

Nothing in the universe travels faster than light. Moving through space about 186,000 miles every second, it crosses enormous distances in a given time period, whether it’s a second, a day, or a year. This is true for any type of electromagnetic radiation, including visible light, microwaves, radio waves, gamma rays, X-rays, or infrared. A light-day is the distance that light will travel in 24 hours, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). 

To put this mileage into perspective, consider some other light-distances: 

  • The Moon is 238,855 miles (384,400 kilometers) from Earth, on average. The astronauts on the Artemis II mission took about three days to get there, but light can traverse that distance in 1.3 seconds.
  • Sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 93 million miles from the Sun to Earth (about 150 million kilometers), meaning our nearest star is about 8.3 light-minutes away. 
  • The distance between Earth and Mars changes as they orbit the Sun, and it can take anywhere from three minutes to 22 minutes for light to travel between the two planets. Same for a radio transmission, either to or from a spacecraft at Mars. 
  • Neptune, the most distant planet in our solar system, with an average distance from Earth of about 2.8 billion miles (4.5 billion kilometers), is four light-hours and 10 light-minutes away. It took Voyager 2, traveling about 35,000 miles per hour, 12 years to reach Neptune.

That’s why light-year — how far light can travel in a year — is used to measure and convey the vastness of space. It’s about 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). The closest neighboring solar system to our own, the star Proxima Centauri and its one or more planets, is about 4.24 light-years away (or, about 24.95 trillion miles, or 40.15 trillion kilometers). And the next-closest galaxy to our own Milky Way, the Andromeda galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.

Where is Voyager 1 going?

Voyager 1 is headed in the direction of a star more than 17 light-years away from Earth called AC +79 3888, also known as Gliese 445. It’s an obscure star now in the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear or Little Dipper), and Voyager 1 is expected to pass within about 1.7 light-years of it — in 40,000 years. Even though the spacecraft, in flight since 1977, is cruising at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) through the vacuum of space, that’s a relative crawl compared to the speed of light.

When Voyager 1 makes its mark Nov. 18, the spacecraft will have taken 49 years, two months, and 11 days to have traveled one light-day beyond Earth — a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating.

Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now?

Check the cosmic odometer for each spacecraft, and watch the miles roll over by the second — in real time.

What has it discovered in its nearly 50-year journey? Which of its instruments are still operating? Learn more about the Pale Blue Dot and the Golden Record.

Listen to Episode 61 of "We Asked a NASA Expert." (Spoiler: in getting to an answer, "things get really weird.")

The space beyond Earth is so incredibly vast that, when expressed in miles and kilometers — the units of measure from our everyday lives — the numbers grow impossibly big.
