items.content:
Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem.

ParticleDB aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called . To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces, including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics.

ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor. Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai. Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4.

While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior.

ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.

ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The mode called on each commit, batched multiple transactions into a single , and skipped altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described as offering “stronger durability” than . On the other hand, said the mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator guide concurred: offered the “same durability as ”.

ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.” However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”, which is not fully isolated.

Most SQL databases use the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement to control the concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB ignored or rejected these statements. In some cases it instructed users to choose , a relatively weak isolation level. In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary).

Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the setting passed at startup. The transaction engine documentation described four modes:

No locks; commit-on-writeBulk loads, single-writer benchmarks
Overlay + commit-time OCC validation (default)General OLTP — safe under concurrency
Partition-pinned OCC; single-partition txns skip cross-partition coordinationHigh-throughput OLTP on partition-affine workloads (TPC-C, key-value)
Exclusive table locks at first touchStrictest serialization, simple semantics

This table was difficult to interpret. While the best practices documentation warned that users should “pick deliberately”, since “it changes correctness and throughput characteristics more than SQL text does”, the documentation did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The mode was similarly unclear. “Commit-time OCC validation” could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but “safe under concurrency” suggests it might be Serializable. The mode described a performance optimization which could be as safe as , but it was described as “safe under concurrency”—raising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally, if offered the “strictest serialization”, was some weaker isolation level?

The CLI reference page contained another table which described and as “Jepsen-safe”, whereas was not “Jepsen-safe”, but did not explain their safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret these terms.

Running provided the following table:

No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe under concurrency)
Table locks + commit-time validation (safe for most OLTP)
Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput safe mode)
Exclusive table locks, full serialization (strictest)
Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding — see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md)

The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a alias was surprising. Moreover, “safe for most OLTP” undermines the claim that was “safe under concurrency”; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads which are unsafe!

Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong: was actually optimistic, and the alias was to preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions of the various transaction modes. This document was difficult to interpret, but did specify the following consistency models:

(a.k.a. , , )
(a.k.a. )
(a.k.a. )
(a.k.a. )

Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes, but in general, and appeared to be the default.

We wrote a test suite for ParticleDB using the Jepsen testing library. We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of un-ed writes using LazyFS, and truncate or corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and all three WAL sync modes.

We first tried ParticleDB’s official Java SDK. While the documentation indicated that the library was available as a Maven dependency, neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later added support for the ParticleDB Java SDK, versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2.

We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB.

The workload performed randomly generated transactions involving reads and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer constraints on the version orders and transaction dependency graphs. Jepsen’s transactional checker, Elle, then searched for cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic phenomena like G1a (Aborted Read).

The workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a comma-separated field, and used SQL to append to them. Rows could be selected via primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic phenomena.

When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single transaction, we designed an workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a series of randomly generated transactions involving , , , and statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each individual transaction, reads observed prior writes.

To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the workload, we designed the workload. This workload used Clojure’s test.check generative testing library to produce random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDB’s behavior was not equivalent to PostgreSQL’s, the compare workload would search for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simple—just a few basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic, transactions, and some simple , , and clauses—it proved remarkably fruitful.

Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more complex transactions. This workload generated a random set of tables, then concurrently executed random transactions over them. It then checked each transaction independently to ensure that each of its statements observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a transaction executed , then observed a row with , we could prove that transaction was not internally consistent.

We found 96 issues with ParticleDB, which we present in several categories below. All but three of these issues occurred in healthy, single-node instances of ParticleDB. Busy readers may wish to jump to the Discussion section, which summarizes our findings.

Under normal operation, ParticleDB was slow, deadlocked, and crashed without warning.

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, was so slow as to be essentially unusable. While some transactions might complete in a few milliseconds, most took 10, 20, or even 30 seconds, then failed.

For example, take this test run with a single node running 1.1.18.4, transaction mode , and WAL mode . With ten concurrent clients, most transactions blocked for tens of seconds before throwing could not serialize access due to concurrent update, or an IO error.

High latencies (#62) appeared improved by 1.1.18.6, which could execute transactions with sub-100 millisecond latencies for at least a few seconds.

While 1.1.18.6 improved latencies, it also crashed frequently. Crashes occurred spontaneously with various transaction modes, WAL modes, and client interfaces; there was no obvious cause. Nodes would run for a few hundred to a few thousand seconds before exiting. No error messages were printed. These crashes (#81) no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

Deadlock After Two Transactions (#27)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.8, submitting as few as two concurrent transactions to a healthy, single-node deployment could cause it to deadlock. This occurred both using the Postgres and ParticleDB interfaces. The node would log an error message like [DEADLOCK] 1 cycles detected at SystemTime ..., and an empty backtrace. In some cases new clients could attach and perform transactions; in others, new clients would also hang indefinitely. This may reflect multiple deadlock bugs.

With the workload, version 1.1.18.9 generally could not run for more than 45 seconds without locking up. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 could reliably run for two minutes without lockups, and we declared the issue (#27) resolved.

Deadlock With (#71)

While version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 fixed the most frequent deadlocks, we continued to find deadlocks through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 when running with . An otherwise healthy ParticleDB node would execute transactions for about 30 seconds, then get stuck forever. The node would log a similar deadlock error message to #27, and all requests with the ParticleDB client would throw after a 100 second default timeout. These deadlocks (#71) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-7.

Orkes’ public documentation claimed broad support for Postgres features, and the internal operator guide concurred:

The engine speaks PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol natively — anything that speaks pgjdbc / libpq / psycopg2 / pq connects unchanged. , , , prepared statements, parameterised queries, and extended-query pipelining all work as expected.

These claims were somewhat optimistic. ParticleDB was missing support for a wide array of Postgres features, and others were badly broken.

No Aggregates Within (#20)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, aggregate expressions like were not supported within expressions.

This threw Error: cannot evaluate wildcard expression. ParticleDB gained support for this feature (#20) by version 1.1.18.6.

Unsupported Exponentiation (#28)

ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 did not support the Postgres exponentiation operator:

Version 1.1.18.9 added support for the operator (#28).

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, any attempt to execute a prepared statement using the Postgres JDBC driver caused an exception like Execution error (NoSuchElementException) at java.util.ArrayDeque/removeFirst. Since the JDBC driver automatically switches to prepared statements after the first few calls to , this rendered the database essentially unusable. As a workaround, we disabled the client’s use of prepared statements.

Prepared statements are executed using Postgres’ extended query protocol, which takes place in several (potentially reusable) phases: Parse, Bind, Execute, and so on. Orkes believes that ParticleDB likely failed to return a response for one of those phases, or returned an extra message, causing the client’s queue to underflow. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-1, this issue (#2) appeared fixed.

Most Postgres Queries Fail (#83)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-7 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, many queries using the Postgres interface threw Bad value for type long: some_column. This rendered the database largely unusable.

Orkes believes this issue (#83) was fixed in 1.1.19-rc.12.

Tuples Without Fields (#111)

In 1.1.18.11.rc-18 and rc-19, queries with the Postgres interface occasionally threw errors like Received resultset tuples, but no field structure for them. For example, take this test of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, with no faults, a new transaction mode, and WAL mode . It executed a transaction like:

This complained of resultset tuples with no field structure, suggesting an error in ParticleDB’s Postgres protocol state machine. While Jepsen has not tested this version, Orkes reports this issue (#111) was fixed in version 1.1.19-rc.13.

Broken Postgres Authentication (#1)

The Postgres wire protocol usually authenticates clients using a username and password. ParticleDB had a option, but 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 lacked any option to set the username. Some of the documentation indicated the default username was , while otherpages said it was . Neither appeared to work; the only option was to use to disable authentication altogether. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 introduced a option (#1).

Java Client Could Not Execute Transactions (#3)

Version 1.0.0 of the official ParticleDB Java client refused every attempt to execute a transaction. Any call to begin a JDBC transaction, or to execute a statement, would result in an error message: PDB wire error 1064: SQL plan error: transaction/session statements do not produce a query plan.

ParticleDB 1.1.4 could execute transactions via its Postgres interface, but using the official Java SDK was essentially impossible. This issue (#3) seems to have been resolved by ParticleDB 1.1.15.

ParticleDB struggled to interpret predicates. clauses failed to match rows they should have, or matched unexpected or nonexistent rows. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

Ignores Clause (#40)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, queries without a table accepted a clause, but ignored it.

This should have returned zero rows. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved this issue (#40).

Version 1.1.1.18.9 introduced a new problem with predicates: inside a transaction, a clause which performed sufficiently complex floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows. For example:

The same problem applied to , , and : predicates like WHERE (a * 2) IS NOT NULL would silently fail to match. However, simpler predicates like would match correctly. The effect disappeared if the column was an integer. Moreover, some predicates which would throw errors outside a transaction would silently match zero rows within a transaction, suggesting these predicates were not being evaluated at all:

This issue (#47) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-1.

ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 aggressively interpreted as a primary-key lookup of , regardless of the value of .

ParticleDB would ignore a row with in favor of :

You could write predicates over non-existent columns:

By version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB had learned that not every equality comparison involved a primary key (#18).

in a Transaction Returns Nonsense (#35)

The behavior of within a transaction in ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 was thoroughly confusing. Consider a single client connected to a fresh single-node instance of ParticleDB 1.1.18.8. It creates a simple table of integers with two rows, and , and begins a transaction:

So far, so good. But now consider:

One might conclude that every with a predicate returned a single row from the requested table—perhaps the most recently inserted row. But this is not true, because many predicates evaluating to returned nothing.

This behavior (#35) seemed improved by ParticleDB 1.1.18.9.

ParticleDB often violated constraints like or , even with a single server, single client, and no faults.

Not-Null Constraints Allow Null (#8)

While ParticleDB allowed users to add constraints to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored them, resulting in bizarre states.

While the resulting row existed in some sense, it was partly invisible.

In version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB started to enforce null constraints (#8).

Unique Constraints Allow Duplicates (#9)

Similarly, while ParticleDB allowed users to add unique constraints to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 simply ignored them.

In version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB partially enforced unique constraints (#9).

Duplicate Primary Keys (#29)

Although 1.1.18.6 made constraints somewhat more robust, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 allowed an to produce multiple rows with the same primary key.

Selecting a row by primary key returned only one of the two rows, but other predicates could return both:

This issue (#29) appears to have been fixed by 1.1.18.9.

Per the SQL standard, primary keys may not be null. This makes intuitive sense, since represents an unknown value. ParticleDB would not allow you to insert null values for primary keys. However, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 were perfectly happy to the primary key of one (or more!) rows to .

ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 rejected attempts to set primary keys to (#57).

Primary Key Conflicts with Deleted Rows (#82)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-11, a transaction which deleted a row, then inserted a new row with the same primary key, would abort due to a primary key constraint violation. For example:

The second would throw PDB wire error 1064: SQL execution error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint (key=7), but only when using the ParticleDB interface—the Postgres interface was unaffected. Orkes partially addressed this issue (#82) in version 1.1.18.11.rc-9, and fixed another case of it in 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

Lack of Primary Key Conflicts with Extant Rows (#90)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9, a transaction executing concurrently with other transactions could read a row with a primary key, then successfully insert a row with that same primary key. For example, take this test, which created a table with two integer columns:

CREATE TABLE u_14 (b int, a int PRIMARY KEY);

A transaction ran and observed several rows, including . It then ran INSERT INTO u_14 (b, a) VALUES (-27, -1), which should have conflicted with the extant primary key, but succeeded instead. It went on to again, and observed the newly inserted row, but not the previously existent one. This is a violation of internal consistency.

As of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, we no longer observed these internal consistency violations (#90).

ParticleDB struggled to join tables together. The following issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

Can’t Join Integers to Floats (#58)

Even after agreeing that , ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 refused to join two tables on an and a column:

Databases like Postgres would return a single row here, since . ParticleDB gained the ability to join floats to integers (#58) by 1.1.18.11.rc-1.

Incorrect Column Names (#54)

Because two tables can have a column with the same name, SQL databases generally return both table and column names, so you can tell which column belonged to which table. ParticleDB, with both the ParticleDB and Postgres interfaces, neglected to return table names. Instead, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 renamed column in joined tables to , , and so on. Consider the following simple join across two tables and , both with an integer column :

In Postgres this produced rows like:

Here the expression denotes column of table . In ParticleDB, this same query returned:

The table names are completely missing, and ParticleDB has altered the name of column to . Programs which expected typical SQL behavior would throw an error as they attempted to read columns which were not present, or could silently read null values.

ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 no longer munged columns, but the database still omitted table names. The resulting name collisions destroyed information.

While Jepsen has not had a chance to test this version, Orkes claims this issue (#54) was resolved by version 1.1.19-rc.13.

Coercing to Strings (#76)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, joins would coerce some values to strings in ParticleDB’s Postgres interface. For example, consider the following join:

With the ParticleDB interface, this produced the number . With the Postgres interface, it produced the string . This issue (#76) seemed fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-21.

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, outer joins of a non-empty table to an empty one often returned no rows, even though the query should have produced all rows in the non-empty table. For example:

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB correctly returned rows when joining to empty tables (#59).

Many tables in real databases contain columns with identical names, like or . When asked to join two tables like this, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 became severely confused, even when all columns were fully qualified. For example:

This should not have matched anything—there are no rows in table where . Instead ParticleDB matched a row in table which satisfied , then cross-joined it to all rows in . To add insult to injury, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 appeared to swap around the output columns, producing the following table:

If column was of a different type than , ParticleDB would try to coerce the types into compatible forms, producing bizarre error messages or delightfully weird results. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 was much less confused when joining tables containing the same column name (#77).

ParticleDB often wound up with rows that could not be deleted or updated, or which persisted in some (perhaps mangled) form after their deletion. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

In ParticleDB 1.1.17 through 1.1.18.8, it appeared impossible to delete rows within a transaction. For example:

We were unable to find a predicate that allowed one to delete records (#26). Version 1.1.18.9 allowed transactions to mostly delete rows.

1.1.18.9 resolved issue #26, but deleted rows still lingered on in some capacity. While a transaction could not directly select deleted rows, it could observe them via aggregate functions and various predicates.

The row must still be present in some sense, because these aggregate queries could observe its value via predicates. However, trying to read the row directly returned nothing:

Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 no longer allowed shades of deleted records to persist in aggregate queries (#45).

Night of the Living Integers (#23)

In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, updating an integer column could make rows impossible to delete. For example:

While this row appears to contain the integer , that integer is , since the statement provided the value . This row cannot be deleted. It does appear in , and is apparently equal to , rather than . Oddly, updating a row by primary key with the same value did not create zombies; the problem (#23) was somehow linked to predicates. ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 no longer exhibited this behavior.

Tables with a column suffered from a similar problem: they could be updated with integer values, but doing so would produce zombie rows that could neither be updated nor deleted again.

If the double precision column was a primary key, these updates would produce duplicate copies of the updated row. This issue (#84) affected ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, and was fixed in 1.1.18.11.rc-9.

A Ghost is Technically Not a Number (#78)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, values stored in or columns could neither be updated nor deleted.

This issue (#78) did not occur with the shell, but did happen with both ParticleDB and Postgres JDBC clients. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 seems to have fixed the problem.

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, fixed-width strings were unmodifiable unless created with exactly the right number of characters. While ParticleDB would correctly pad the string to , the resulting row could neither be updated nor deleted.

If a fixed-width column was used as a primary key, it could be updated, but only once. Both old and new copies would appear as distinct rows.

Any further attempt to modify those rows would produce a duplicate key error, despite all the values involved being distinct. Fixed-width strings were also incomparable using the operator. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 resolved these issues (#74).

In SQL, the statement destroys a table completely. In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, it left a shadow of the table behind, whose rows would reappear in later tables with the same name and more-or-less compatible schemata. To demonstrate this behavior, let us create a table with a single row:

We then drop the table, and demonstrate that it no longer exists:

If we then create a new table with the same name and a somewhat compatible schema, rows from the deleted table reappear in the new one. However, the resurrected rows are not exactly their former selves. The floating-point value has become the integer .

This behavior (#46) seemed linked to transactions, and no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-3.

ParticleDB had many ways to create values which could not be read, alter values unexpectedly, create rows with incorrect or missing columns, or otherwise corrupt logical state. The issues in this section involved only a single server, single client, and no faults.

Unreadable Infinities (#15)

In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, ParticleDB’s Postgres interface did not correctly serialize floating-point values like . One could write infinite values, but trying to read them would cause the client to throw an error.

With Postgres, this correctly returned the JVM’s value. was serialized correctly. At the shell, stored values came back as , rather than . In version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB serialized infinite values correctly (#15).

Sometimes Converted to 0.0 (#21)

ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 would sometimes (but not always!) convert the floating-point value to . For example:

Delightfully, whether this corruption occurred depended on the order in which rows were inserted. If the first value inserted into the table was , that and later s would be preserved. Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to store correctly (#21).

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could update a column of one type to a column of a different, incompatible type—producing values like or . For example:

In Postgres, this UPDATE would throw ERROR: column "a" is of type text but expression is of type int. ParticleDB refused to this string to an integer (at least in this case), but was perfectly happy to make one equal to the other, resulting in . Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to resolve this issue (#7).

Insert Column Order Table Corruption (#16)

In SQL, one usually inserts a row into a table using a statement like INSERT INTO people (name, age) VALUES ('xanthippe', 15). ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored the statement’s columns, using whatever column order had been used to create the table originally. This produced rows with titillating properties. Consider the following pair of inserts: one with columns in the same order as the table’s schema, and a second in a different order:

While ParticleDB thinks this table contains two rows, neither can be read via :

In general, any query which happened to encounter a row inserted with a different column order would silently produce zero results. However, each row could be read by primary key! Note the different column orders in the output:

The server spontaneously deadlocked (#27, #71) or crashed (#81) every few minutes. Integers stood in for booleans (#30, #50), comparisons to threw errors (#13), and you could assign multiple values to the same column (#5). Large floating-point numbers quietly became infinite (#56); , , and arithmetic were broken (#36, #92, #15, #21); and out-of-range values were improperly stored or clipped to fit (#32, #11). In ParticleDB, was not equal to (#63), but wasn’t equal to (#80). Strings allowed too many (#52, #64) and too few (#55) characters. A clause with floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows (#47), returned rows with primary key (#18), matched the row , and matched nothing (#35). Null (#8) and unique (#9) constraints did nothing, and primary keys could be duplicated (#29), null (#57), or both. Primary keys failed to conflict with rows that did exist (#90), and conflicted with rows that didn’t (#82). Joins returned incorrect column names (#54), coerced values to strings (#76), failed to return rows (#59), and confused similarly-named columns (#77). Queries sometimes missed (#48), duplicated (#89), or returned the wrong (#67) rows. Tables with a primary key were mostly invisible (#41). Special values were sometimes inalterable (#91). Entire columns occasionally vanished for no obvious reason (#65). Uncontended statements on freshly created tables observed nonsensical results or conflicted (apparently) with themselves (#31). Each transaction and WAL mode exhibited essentially every transactional anomaly our tests could detect: write loss, internal consistency violations, G0, G1a, G1b, G1c, G-Single, G-nonadjacent, P4, A5A, G2, and real-time variants thereof (#38, #66, #68, #69, #73, #70, #96, #109, #110, etc.).

These behaviors occurred in single-node instances of ParticleDB, without fault injection, often with just a single client. When we killed ParticleDB, it allowed internal anomalies, P4 (Lost Update), and G-single (#107), even with the new transaction mode. Corruption or truncation of WAL files caused partial data loss (#108). Simulating misdirected reads or writes could cause total data loss (#112).
