As always, Jepsen takes an experimental approach to safety verification: we can prove the presence of bugs, but not their absence. While we make extensive efforts to find problems, we cannot prove correctness.

Orkes believes that the issues we found in 1.1.4 were likely due to an extensive refactor of ParticleDB in spring 2026, and that Orkes and their customers, who continued to run an earlier version, were likely unaffected. Near the end of our collaboration we briefly evaluated an internal build of version 1.0.0. While it exhibited some string and arithmetic issues, that version did not seem susceptible to most of the serious safety errors we found in 1.1.4, and passed cursory and tests. We tested only a single node at a time, so we cannot speak to the safety of the replication system.

From May through July 2026, the ParticleDB download page offered users (at least) versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-18. All exhibited serious safety errors during normal operation. It seems likely that users who ran these versions of ParticleDB would have lost or corrupted data. In version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, using WAL mode and transaction mode significantly reduced the frequency and severity of these issues, but did not prevent internal anomalies or Lost Update.

Given the severity and extent of the safety errors we found, and the process which produced them, Jepsen recommends users halt further deployment of ParticleDB and migrate to other databases as soon as possible. Consider checking and/or rebuilding database state from more reliable sources, if available.

The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Generative Testing

The workload generated random schemas and SQL statements over them, then ran both against ParticleDB and Postgres to see if they produced equivalent results. This should not have worked. There are many ways in which two “Postgres-compatible” databases can legitimately differ, such as floating-point details, which error message takes precedence, or the order of unsorted results. The space of SQL queries is large and difficult to cover. Many queries trivially return equivalent results (e.g. ) and therefore tell us little information. We can test only sequential behavior, which is easy for a database’s standard test suite to check.

Nevertheless, roughly two thousand lines of generative tests found a wealth of bugs in ParticleDB, and unlike Jepsen’s typical workloads, the examples generated were usually easy to reproduce. ParticleDB offered a good deal of “low-hanging fruit” that should have been caught by example-based tests—but the workload also found more subtle errors. For example, the fact that was apparently equal to hinged on a high-precision floating-point literal. Inspired by this success, we extracted part of the ParticleDB SQL generator into a shared library so it could be used in other tests, like the new workload.

Jepsen has traditionally focused on thorough analysis of a small set of carefully chosen transactions. This is partly because checking (e.g.) Serializability in general is NP-complete, and also because we assume that if transactions of (e.g.) reads and appends work correctly on strings, so will other operations on other datatypes. Our intuition is that the “hard part” is in the concurrency control mechanism, and sequential datatype behavior is generally covered by existing tests. This was not the case in ParticleDB. We’ve expanded Jepsen’s and tests to use alternate encodings and transaction structures, in an attempt to cover more codepaths. This revealed new bugs in ParticleDB, and we hope it will in other databases too.

Unfortunately, became less useful as Orkes fixed major bugs and left smaller incompatibilities in place. For example, Postgres checks unique constraints when updating each row of a table, but ParticleDB only checks after all have been updated. This means that a statement like UPDATE bools SET x = NOT x can swap the values of and in ParticleDB without violating a unique constraint. Toward the end of our engagement, the test generally hit these minor inconsistencies early, then spent most of its time searching for minimal cases of them—potentially missing more serious bugs.

Orkes said they ran Jepsen’s existing Postgres test harness to find and resolve issues in ParticleDB prior to this work. However, that same test harness failed immediately when run against ParticleDB 1.1.4. Orkes also stated they tested ParticleDB with SQLancer, which generates far more complex queries than the ones we tested. It is therefore perplexing that nearly every feature we tested exhibited glaring errors, and that our findings seemed to come as a surprise.

Most databases have a test suite which exercises at least basic examples of each feature, and it is customary to run those tests before release, if not continuously. Where were those tests for ParticleDB? How does one add support for constraints without a test which tries to insert at least one value? What development process adds a type without trying to write a string of (e.g.) five characters?

Our findings suggest structural deficiencies in the ParticleDB QA process. Perhaps tests were not run prior to release. Perhaps the test suite was run, but failed to exercise basic functionality. Perhaps engineers entrusted Large Language Models with the work of testing.

Jepsen recommends that Orkes (and all database vendors!) build and exercise an automated test suite for their database. This suite should include at least simple, example-based tests covering important database features. These tests should fail when the feature is unimplemented or malformed, and pass when it is complete. Observing these failures is an important part of the development process: it validates that the test measures something. Tests should be run at least once before each release, and results disseminated to the team. Afterwards consider more sophisticated generative tests, establishing adversarial QA and implementation teams, and subtly breaking safety mechanisms to determine whether the tests are still effective.

ParticleDB’s website gave the appearance of a mature database project. It made strong claims: a general-purpose OLTP/OLAP SQL database a thousand times faster than PostgreSQL, “formally verified” by a TLA+ proof, multiple APIs, and client libraries in thirteen languages. It offered a variety of deployment options and extensive documentation on database features and operations.

On closer inspection, that documentation was riddled with omissions, inconsistencies, and confabulations. The TLA+ proof was not published, and in any event did not prevent disaster—perhaps it was incorrect, formalized the wrong properties, or did not describe the system as built. Safety-critical configuration settings like the transaction mode were described in vague terms, like “safe under concurrency”. The documentation for the Java client library referred to non-existent dependency coordinates and seemed to make up class and package names which were nowhere to be found in the library itself. The quickstart and client examples made up a variety of default usernames for ParticleDB, all of which were wrong. The stored procedure documentation even fabricated an imaginary email address for the author of this report. In Orkes’ unpublished operator guide, the descriptions of transaction modes omitted basic phenomena like G0 and confused G1a (Aborted Read) with G1c (Circular Information Flow). The Snapshot Isolation modes made no mention of G-single or the other boundary phenomena proscribed by Snapshot Isolation, and non-real-time models made no mention of the real-time phenomena they allowed, like Stale Read.

Technical writing is important work that requires skill and care. Jepsen recommends that Orkes work with a human technical writer to rewrite ParticleDB’s documentation, with an eye toward concisely and accurately communicating intended behavior and the guarantees users should expect.

Jepsen is no stranger to working with early software projects, and there is nothing intrinsically wrong with offering buggy or badly broken software. However, it would be polite for a maintainer aware of serious safety issues to display a prominent warning on the website. One might place a large red box on the download page which reads, “This project is in early development and is not suitable for production”, or more bluntly, “This software has lost data and will do so again”. Orkes should clearly explain the general status of ParticleDB, and advise users of specific known safety issues.

Orkes has since published a release history which describes versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 as “unsupported pre-release builds”. It is not clear how users would have understood versions like 1.1.4 or 1.1.18.9 as “pre-release”. Pre-release software generally has a version number beginning with 0, or including “rc”, “alpha”, etc. The documentation did not describe these versions as pre-release or experimental at the time. Indeed, the Docker install page told users how to deploy these versions “for production”.

Large Language Models enable small teams to produce software and documentation of staggering scope and complexity in a remarkably short time. Five years ago, writing a distributed SQL database of this scope might have taken hundreds of person-years. With LLM assistance, a handful of engineers at Orkes were able to produce a highly sophisticated database system.

However, our work on ParticleDB (and other databases) suggests there are serious tradeoffs to relying on LLMs. Quality suffered: ParticleDB was a fractal of correctness errors. LLM tooling repeatedly claimed that bugs had been fixed when, in fact, they had not. ParticleDB also seemed more difficult to understand than typical databases. As with most Jepsen analyses, Orkes engineers offered detailed explanations of the causes and resolutions of the bugs we found in Conductor. However, Orkes seemed unable to explain the causes or resolutions of nearly every issue we found in ParticleDB. New builds simply materialized, sans changelogs, each hopefully containing a slew of improvements. Why did ParticleDB sometimes turn strings into integers? Why did it stop in 1.1.18.11.rc-1? Perhaps no one knows. With LLMs, perhaps no one needs to.

More broadly, the use of LLMs erodes trust in documentation, in software, and in the organizations which produce them. Perhaps engineers will begin to treat any new software project with suspicion—the signals we used to rely on as markers of a mature system are now easier to counterfeit.

Where correctness matters—and surely it ought to matter for databases!—our industry must acknowledge and mitigate these tradeoffs. In the age of LLMs, what can maintainers do to ensure correct software and accurate documentation? Having done that work, how can they demonstrate its quality to users?

As of 1.1.18.11.rc-22, our and workloads were still finding anomalies in every transaction mode. We recommend further testing as development continues. The workload also revealed a number of minor compatibility bugs which we have not discussed here. These small differences could mask more serious errors. Bringing ParticleDB into closer alignment with Postgres could help the workload reveal them.

Toward the end of our collaboration we tested ParticleDB’s on-disk format, and found that corruption in WAL files could cause data loss. The variety of error messages we found suggests that there might be multiple paths to data loss—further tests should stress on-disk storage more thoroughly. Furthermore, in almost all our tests ParticleDB wrote only WAL files, and stored its tables entirely in memory. We recommend Orkes add a configuration option to reduce the thresholds for on-disk storage, so that future tests can exercise those codepaths.

The ParticleDB client has a number of slow network timeouts we did not know how to change. These timeouts could conceal safety errors by preventing the test from observing the database during a critical moment. We worked around this by using the Postgres client (whose timeouts are configurable), but we recommend testing the ParticleDB client with lower timeouts as well.

ParticleDB offered a massive set of features, and we only tested a small portion of them. The SQL specification and Postgres’ dialect of it are astonishingly complex languages, and we used only a small fraction of their syntax and vocabulary. We also did not evaluate ParticleDB’s Redis or HTTP APIs, temporal or geospatial queries, materialized views, vector search, or multi-tenant features. The replication system remains to be tested.

Orkes is now adding stored procedures to ParticleDB. These user-defined functions, called , are written in Python or Rust and executed by the database server. Both Rust and Python have large surface areas, and executing user-provided binaries in a database environment seems like an exciting opportunity. Our previous work with stored procedures suggests this feature is worth further investigation.

ParticleDB claimed to be “1087x faster than PostgreSQL”. In our tests ParticleDB was nowhere near this fast, and over the course of an hour we observed a linear decline in throughput and a significant increase in median latencies—even over small datasets. Once ParticleDB reaches a baseline level of correctness, revisiting performance benchmarks could be worthwhile.

Our thanks to the ParticleDB team at Orkes, including Jeu George and Nikhil Kala. Jepsen also wishes to thank Irene Kannyo for her editorial support. This research was funded by Orkes, Inc., and conducted in accordance with the Jepsen ethics policy.

This appendix contains additional results involving types, syntax, numbers, and strings.

We found several incompatibilities or bugs involving static or dynamic type safety, or behaviors that would normally have been caught by static analysis of a query, such as referring to a nonexistent column. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

Ordering By an Unused Column (#33)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could order an aggregate query’s results by a column that was not used in the aggregate expressions or clause. This seems like a minor issue, but it does differ from Postgres behavior:

Orkes resolved this issue (#33) in 1.1.18.9.

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could write predicates for and which made equality comparisons between columns of different types.

In Postgres, this threw an error like ERROR: operator does not exist: text = smallint. You could compare strings to boolean columns, or literal values like . ParticleDB allowed these comparisons on empty tables, but would throw an error if a record was present. In 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB threw an error for empty tables as well (#6).

ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2 forgot how to compare large decimal literals to 64-bit floating-point numbers:

This issue (#94) no longer appeared by version 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

Filter Predicates Reject (#12)

SQL has three boolean values: , , and , which represents an unknown value. In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, predicates in SELECT, UPDATE, etc. could not evaluate to , even though the SQL specification states that search conditions are boolean expressions. For example:

In Postgres this would return an empty relation, because is not . In 1.1.18.6, predicates evaluated correctly (#12).

Per the ANSI SQL standard, the value of comparing anything to is , represented as the boolean value . However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 sometimes refused to evaluate predicates which compared (e.g.) integers to .

Oddly enough, ParticleDB correctly evaluated statements like . Version 1.1.18.6 correctly compared integers to (#13).

Boolean Logic on Integers (#30)

The SQL standard is clear that boolean logical expressions like evaluate to booleans. In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, they could sometimes be other things:

By version 1.1.18.9, ParticleDB rejected boolean expressions over non-boolean literals (#30).

More Boolean/Integer Confusion (#50)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 disallowed boolean logic on integer literals, but allowed it on columns.

Likewise, you could do integer operations on booleans:

Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#50) by version 1.1.18.11.rc-8.

Multiple Assignment to a Single Column (#5)

The SQL standard specifies that an statement shall not contain a column name more than once. However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 allowed an to assign multiple values to the same column. It seemed to pick the last value, lexically.

In Postgres this returned an error: multiple assignments to same column "a". However, ParticleDB applied the update, producing:

By version 1.1.18.6, multiple updates to the same column threw an error (#5).

Predicates Referring to Non-Existent Columns (#10)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, predicates in , , and statements could refer to columns which did not exist. For example:

In Postgres, expressions like this would throw ERROR: column "b" does not exist. By version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB did as well (#10).

ParticleDB often performed arithmetic in unexpected ways. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

No Large Integer Literals (#14)

Postgres allows large integer literals like (). However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 refused these literals, throwing an error:

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.6, one could write large integer literals (#14).

To Infinity, and Beyond (#85)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 gained an exponentiation operator , but could not apply it to .

This returned in Postgres, but threw operator does not exist: ^ requires numeric operands in ParticleDB. By 1.1.18.11.rc-9, Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#85).

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 considered to be equal to , rather than .

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, it correctly returned (#49).

ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 gained support for literals using scientific notation—for example, using to denote . However, the parser turned this notation into floating-point values, rather than precise decimals, as in Postgres. This resulted in floating-point errors:

This issue (#88) was fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2.

What’s the Largest Number You Can Think Of? (#56)

ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 silently converted large floating-point literals to infinities:

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an error like "4.56E500" is out of range for type double precision (#56).

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the exponent operator checked to see if its arguments would cause an overflow, but did not check for underflow:

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an underflow error (#61).

Division by Integer Zero (#34)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could divide floating-point values by integer and receive , rather than a error, as in Postgres.

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 returned an error instead (#34).

Modulo Operator Cannot Handle Floats (#51)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the modulo operator threw an internal error when either argument was a floating-point number.

The function was unaffected, and this issue (#51) was fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-1.

Broken Arithmetic (#36)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, arithmetic operations on would throw an error:

By 1.1.18.9, arithmetic on correctly returned (#36).

Broken Arithmetic (#92)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2, arithmetic operations involving sufficiently detailed scientific notation literals and threw internal errors:

This error (#92) no longer appeared in version 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

UPDATE Can’t Do Math (#60)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which rendered it unable to do arithmetic operations on floating-point columns in an statement. For example:

In 1.1.18.11.rc-1, ParticleDB was (mostly) able to add numbers (#60).

Same Precision For and (#32)

Per the SQL standard, the data type should have a greater precision than . In Postgres, and are (usually) a 32-bit and 64-bit floating-point value, respectively. In ParticleDB, both appear to be implemented as 64-bit floats.

Version 1.1.18.9 seemed to introduce a 32-bit type (#32).

Similarly, integer fields (e.g. , , …) in ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 allowed values much bigger than their typical ranges. It appeared as if ParticleDB internally represented all integer types as signed 64-bit integers. For example, here are four values too big to fit in a Postgres :

In Postgres is a 16-bit integer; each would throw ERROR: smallint out of range. However, ParticleDB stored each of these values with varying results. It preserved 32,768 and (the largest two’s-complement signed 64-bit integer). and larger integers were silently converted to . On the other hand, the large floating-point number was clipped to .

Similar behavior occurred with and . ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 rejected oversized integers (#11).

Dividing Nearby Numbers (#86)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8 struggled to divide floating-point numbers, often throwing when asked to divide values which were well within the range of a 32-bit float. For example:

This value should be approximately . Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#86) in version 1.1.18.11.rc-9.

Floating-Point Errors in Integer Values (#87)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, adding small numbers (e.g. ) to large integer columns could cause their values to change by surprising amounts. For example:

Adding to this column actually subtracted . Jepsen suspects this bug (#87) was caused by performing these operations on floating-point values (which cannot represent all integers) then coercing the result back to the nearest integer value. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have fixed this.

Postgres considers floating-point numbers like to be equal to their quoted representations—this is useful because some floating-point values, like , are written with quotes. ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 thought otherwise:

This issue (#19) appeared resolved as of version 1.1.18.6.

Floats Are Not Equal to Integers (#63)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.6, floats were not equal to integers.

By version 1.1.18.8, reasonably-sized integers were equal to their floating-point counterparts (#63).

Double Precision Floats Appear Equal to Almost All Integers (#80)

Version 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which made predicates like fail to match for most double precision floats in (-1.0, 1.0). It was as if all small floats were equal to all nonzero integers. If we took a table containing a few integers, and performed some simple queries that should return every row…

All three of these queries returned only a single row, —implying that was equal to and . The only exception seemed to be , which returned no rows at all. This was also wrong, but somewhat less so. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have resolved the matter (#80).

We found several problems with strings in ParticleDB, including datatypes that could hold more or fewer characters than they ought, and improper sort orders. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

Allows More Than Characters (#64, #52)

The SQL standard defines a variety of fixed-width string datatypes like , which holds a string of exactly three characters. Unfortunately, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 were happy to store much larger strings in those columns.

Version 1.1.18.6 rejected inserts and updates of too-long string literals (#64), but appeared to perform these checks only at runtime; one could still say UPDATE t SET a = 'far too long' so long as it matched no rows (#52). That issue was resolved in version 1.1.18.11.rc-3.

Allows Fewer Than Characters (#55)

While 1.1.18.6 rejected strings that were too large for a fixed-width string column, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 also allowed strings that were too short. Normally, shorter strings are padded with spaces to the specified length, but in ParticleDB, short strings were returned unchanged.

This should have returned , with padding spaces. ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved the issue (#55).

Default Text Collation (#22)

On a platform with , Postgres uses that collation by default. ParticleDB appeared to collate strings differently. Sorting via queries like , or comparisons like , returned different results between the two databases. Where Postgres considered , ParticleDB believed the opposite.

Experiments suggest ParticleDB sorted by Unicode code point order, rather than the Unicode Collation Algorithm (UCA) with the locale’s collation rules. It may have been compatible with , , or . ParticleDB version 1.1.18.9 seemed to choose a default collation more like UCA (#22).

Mis-Sorted Text (#42, #93)

Throughout our collaboration ParticleDB struggled to sort things. Versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 accepted an explicit text collation, then ignored it:

In Postgres’ collation, letters like and sort similarly, despite being of different cases. This query would have returned .

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 sorted English uppercase and lowercase letters correctly, but only for some queries—adding a clause to a statement would cause it to revert to the old sort order. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 resolved that, but sorted other characters, like punctuation, oddly:

Different sorting of whitespace and punctuation (#42) seemed better in version 1.1.18.11.rc-7, but reappeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19 (#93). Text sorting seemed improved in 1.1.18.11.rc-21.

items.title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
Prospero: A new coding harness for a more civilized age
items.content:
nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/

I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now. The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular, higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued to . This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own: . It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear ImGui docking interface. It uses around two orders of magnitude fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features.

Dark mode aficionados are covered, too:

Note that Prospero comes with no model providers built-in. You’re expected to supply that yourself, such as with llama.cpp, a workplace on-prem model, OpenRouter, Anthropic API, OpenAI API, etc. (You can’t use your Claude subscription.)

For those unfamiliar with coding harnesses: In a chat interface you and the AI take turns writing messages to each other. A coding harness extends this concept, allowing an AI to “talk” to tools offered by the harness. Tools “reply” with their outputs. A tool might read or write a file, or run a shell command. An AI will go from tool call to tool call on its own, looping on the results. Such an AI is called an . Occasionally the AI will send you a message to inform you of progress or to ask a question, and the chat interface is still there.

Some harnesses, including Prospero, allow agents to spawn to do their bidding, to work in parallel or keep their clean. That is, to not fill their working memory with subtasks. Agents can message one another and coordinate on tasks. Given SSH access to another machine, or over plain WSL, Prospero can deploy a headless copy of itself to other hosts so that agents can operate on those systems. The Professional Edition embeds engines for combinations of x86/x86-64 and ARM64 on macOS, Windows, and Linux. The Windows x86 engine even works on Windows XP, and can play solitaire and minesweeper if you ask.

The last is because Prospero is one of the few harnesses with capabilities. If your model supports vision — any any model worth using does — then it can “see” your desktop and interact with it. It can click, type, and drag to test and debug GUI applications live without a specialized, per-app MCP assist.

This headless engine is why no TUI is necessary. The harness engine runs on the headless system, and the UI runs on your desktop or laptop. With a little extra setup, the harness to run fully independently of the GUI, so that it will continue without the GUI system attached — re-attachable later.

Because Prospero is so lean, it may be the only harness that can drive a fuzz campaign, particularly on a headless system, without the Linux OOM killer targeting the memory-gobbling harness rather than the out-of-control fuzz target that triggered it. So many times I’ve checked back in on a fuzz campaign hours later, to find nothing was accomplished because the harness process is gone.

(Why have an agent run a fuzz campaign? Because it can fix discovered bugs on the fly and keep the campaign going! It’s a no brainer.)

The configuration lives at ~/.config/prospero/prospero.ini. Easy to edit. No JSON, thank goodness. Check it into source control, copy-paste it. All the usual benefits. Alternatively, the Settings page can reach every setting from the GUI, so you don’t have to edit the INI by hand. INI files can also include each other, not just naming file system paths but URLs:

 = https://example.com/prospero.ini

The idea is to allow a live shared or managed configuration. Includes by URL are restricted in what they can set, with a hard rule against anything which might appear in shell command. Some trust is still required, as a configuration can extract an environment variable by using it as an API key and supplying an endpoint it controls.

Prospero fetches a model list and other parameters like context size from the endpoint, but you might want to tweak it. A typical configuration may look like:

 = falstaff/Qwen3.8-27B

 = http://falstaff.local/
 = env:FALSTAFF_API_KEY

 = replace
 = medium

 = Qwen3.8-27B
 = xhigh

 = searxng
 = https://search.example.com/
 = env:EXAMPLE_API_KEY

The ImGui paradigm typically uses , redrawing on vsync like a video game. This is appropriate in some contexts, like interfaces within video games. Less so for mostly-static text-oriented UIs, such as a coding harness. Instead Prospero uses with to finish animations before going idle. When there’s nothing to do, Prospero does nothing. It won’t chew on the GPU while the agent is waiting on a build.

An annoyance with most other harnesses is how easily they get stuck. I set a long-running task, go to sleep, and in the morning find the harness hung on a trivial issue two hours into the night, wasting the rest. Therefore Prospero prime design principle: . Every operation has a deadline. This decision influences everything. If you’re not there to grant a requested permission, the agent will get a denial by timeout and must do without. To assist, Prospero will raise a system toast when an agent requires your attention so that you’re less likely to miss it if you’re attending.

The harness itself plows through intermittent errors, trying its best to drive the agent to complete its task. All network requests have timeouts, and watchdogs prevent endless waiting. Agent mailboxes are bounded.

Shell commands that hit their timeout convert to asynchronous background commands. The agent can continue to wait on them, with a timeout, and so will be woken at regular intervals to decide if it should continue.

The one exception is Plan mode, where it waits indefinitely after offering a plan or requesting clarification ( tool). It’s expected that a user is attending to the agent during Plan mode.

The harnesses I’ve used have improved, but another regular annoyance earlier this year was agents starting processes that never get cleaned up. An agent kicks off a parallel build, hits a timeout because it was too optimistic, the build “stops” by killing a piece of the build system. But actually the build continues anyway, at least in part. The agent tries again, and now two builds are going, interfering with each other, making a mess and bringing my system to its knees.

For awhile I was wary of letting agents run builds in certain harnesses, which is a terrible outcome. You want agents to close the loop and iterate independently. A human in the loop is like putting a ball and chain on the agent, giving up most of its advantages.

Prospero promoting a synchronous timeout to an asynchronous task is a huge improvement on its own, but there’s an additional principle at play: The whole process tree lives and dies together. When a command is stopped, . This is trivial on Windows, though few harnesses seem to take advantage of it. It’s more difficult on macOS and Linux, but Prospero follows through.

Like every harness, Prospero supports , a pre-packaged set of instructions on how to accomplish some task (“I know kung fu.”). Prospero contains a skill on itself and can read its built-in documentation. Ask the agent how to do or configure something in Prospero, and the agent can only answers your question, it can provide a hyperlink taking you to the relevant place in the UI. It can also edit your and reload it, to configure things on your behalf. This is not unique to Prospero, but I’m not aware of any harness doing this nearly as well.

On Windows, Prospero is designed to work well with w64devkit, and will prefer its shell if available. Models designed for coding know w64devkit out-of-the-box, so these tools are complementary. Of course you’re not locked into that shell, and you can freely choose a different default shell. But Prospero is a rare harness where you can change shells mid session. Sometimes PowerShell is more suited to the task, so you can pick it out of the dropdown. The agent is informed of the change, and told about known quirks (i.e. “this is an old Bash!”). On macOS you can switch between bash and zsh.

Prospero has the usual sorts of features you can expect from an advanced shell. It can use Git worktrees, including subagent worktrees, so that agents can share a repository. It speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It can search the web (if you allow). You can start side chats that share context, realized as subagents. You can fork sessions.

For now there is no built-in terminal or editor. Instead Prospero will open an external terminal or editor of your choosing. I’d rather use Vim than a built-in notepad.exe-equivalent. With Ctrl+G you can edit your prompt in an external editor.

Like all harnesses, the permissions system will not stop a malicious agent. Agents are writing and running programs on your computer, and so can ultimately access everything the harness can access. Permissions are about gently reminding the agent of your wishes, and catching simple mistakes. More like, “Whoa there, stay within the project” or, “Do not control my desktop at this time.” If you want to lock an agent out, you have to restrict the harness itself, putting it in a container or on a Raspberry Pi, at the usual cost of inconvenience or cutting off useful resources.

I’m really excited about Prospero, and I honestly feel it’s one of the best coding harnesses available. It’s how such tools ought to be built, but until now nobody else stepped up to do it. It would take a video to do it justice, and maybe I’ll do that sometime, but that’s currently outside my experience.

Most of the audience for my projects are hobbyists, even w64devkit. But if Prospero goes beyond me and my little circle, I expect most users would be professionals building commercial products. I’ve also invested more than just my time into this project — already true for w64devkit, even more true with Prospero. So while it’s an open source project, I’ve split it into two tiers:

  • Community Edition: the build you find on GitHub at no cost. It has no built-in headless engines, so remote deployments are limited. Plus a little nag text to remind you you’re on the Community Edition. Suited for hobbyists.

  • Professional Edition: Pay a nominal fee, get a DRM-free download with free updates. All the headless engines are built in so you can push remote deployments and remote sessions on other systems at the press of a button. A serious feature for professionals.

Windows and macOS builds are code-signed in both cases (some of the cost). If Prospero is useful for you professionally, even without the remote deployment feature, you’re still encouraged to buy a copy to support my ongoing costs!

items.title: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
items.content:
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

The message that should not have worked

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of , which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.

This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through do not automatically run.

The next step was an using , a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

The response began like this:

Ending our callback with made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.

Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.

We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.

The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:

    The resulting link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

    We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

    The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

    At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.

    At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as , which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

    The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:

    GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2

    This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.

    Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

    We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

    The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

    Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.

    What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

    The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

    Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

      The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

      OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

      The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

        This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.

        Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code.
        Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript.
        Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click.
        Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh.
        Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program.
        Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof.
        OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1.
        OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated.
        CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained.
        OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.

        The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.

        The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:

        Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:

        acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

        The parser and CSP transition. The operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted in .

        The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with consumed the error object appended by the endpoint.

        For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with , double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside , and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters.

        The same-origin frame parsed from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers:

        Authorization: Bearer <victim token>
ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account>
Accept: application/json

        The primary requests were:

        GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true

        Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers.

          The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.

Much Ado About None: Sentinel Values in Python
items.content:
is probably the most overloaded value in Python. We use it as a Swiss Army knife to express that something is , , that an occurred, or simply as an actual value. In my talk about sentinel values, which I presented this year at PyConDE/PyData Berlin 2026, EuroPython 2026 and, most recently, the Swiss Python Summit 2026, I take a closer look at why this ambiguity bites us and what to use instead.

The problem shows up in many places. A simple cache returns both for a missing key and for a key that maps to . Does in a configuration update mean “no timeout” or “keep the current value”? And a function that swallows a and returns uses it as an error signal. Sentinel values resolve this by being a guard the domain of valid values, so they can never collide with an actual value.

Python itself relies heavily on sentinels, hidden in plain sight: skips dimensions in NumPy slicing and marks stubs, and means “find the implementation somewhere else”, which enables double dispatch for binary operators via methods like . Pydantic’s distinguishes a field that was explicitly set to from one that was never sent at all, and it has just left the experimental stage in Pydantic 2.14.

Things get tricky once you create your own sentinels. The classic works perfectly at runtime but breaks type narrowing in static type checkers. Workarounds like guards, magic strings or the single-member trick all come with trade-offs, and identity checks break when sentinels are copied or pickled.

Then came a plot twist. At PyConDE in April, I had to conclude that 661, the proposal to standardize sentinels, was deferred. Only nine days later, the Steering Council accepted it. Since Python 3.15, is a built-in, and type checkers can narrow it just like :

If you are on an older Python version, typing_extensions provides a backport. Type-checker support is still catching up, so check your type checker before relying on it.
My main takeaway: be aware of the ambiguity of  and think about what you actually want to express. Use sentinels to resolve the ambiguity, prefer the ones your library already provides, and replace the old  and  hacks with the new built-in. If you are tempted to return  instead of raising an exception, my talk on exceptions and result types might also interest you.
