By Ibuki Omatsu, Anhad Singh, Jacob Lorentzon, Ron Williams on

Last year, the Redox team received a grant to develop io_uring-like Ring Buffer support at the system task level, as a first step towards ring buffer communications between the application and the majority of system services. This phase of the work finished up in September, as the last pieces were put in place.

The team has done a fantastic job, and I want to congratulate Ibuki, Anhad and Jacob, and thank them for their time and effort.

In addition to implementing the Ring Buffer machinery for our system services and drivers that can support it, an and -like API for applications was completed and demonstrated. There was also substantial work done on support crates, including an async executor for drivers.

And there was some very exciting work on various performance improvements, to allow much faster switching between applications and their system services. But I will let the team tell you all the technical details.

Historically asynchronous I/O on Linux was done through the kernel’s native AIO interface. AIO is mainly useful for unbuffered () I/O, and buffered requests silently block. Developers also raised concerns about its complexity and performance. There is also POSIX AIO, but developers often consider its implementation lackluster and slow. To address these problems, several alternative asynchronous mechanisms such as fibrils and syslets/threadlets were proposed but were never merged into the mainline Linux kernel. In early 2019, Jens Axboe proposed and developed the io_uring interface, designed to be an efficient, extensible and “easy to use, hard to misuse.” In its early days, io_uring did have a few security issues and memory leaks, but these have since been addressed. It was merged in Linux 5.1 and is widely used today.

The Linux io_uring interface allows the user to submit one or more I/O operations to the kernel, which are then processed in an asynchronous fashion without blocking the userspace process. Redox, being a microkernel, handles I/O in userspace processes rather than in the kernel. Each stores a handle to its scheme, so an I/O system call on that file can forward the request to the scheme. The async I/O interface developed in this project, called Redox Rings, uses a mechanism similar to io_uring. However, unlike io_uring which is used to submit operations to the kernel, the Redox Rings interface is used by the application to directly submit requests to the appropriate scheme asynchronously without blocking the application. Additionally, the interface allows I/O requests to be issued without any memory copies, by having a separate shared memory region between the scheme and the application (which can be requested as DMA-capable memory).

For portability, the Redox Rings API is designed to be similar to that of liburing and can also be used for general inter-process communication. For example it is used for communication between the RedoxFS filesystem service and NVMed which is the storage driver. The addition of this API has allowed several parts of Redox to reap significant performance improvements!

A ring buffer is a circular queue backed by an array. The interface makes use of two ring buffers which are shared between the application and the scheme:

  • SQ: , where the application writes requests and the scheme reads them
  • CQ: , where the scheme writes responses and the application reads them
  • SQE / CQE: / , entries in the SQ and CQ, respectively
  • Buffer pool: A contiguous block of memory, shared between the application and the scheme, from which data buffers are allocated
  • Data buffer: For a request, we currently support a single data buffer, which is a slice of the contiguous buffer pool, defined by an offset and length

Since each queue has exactly one producer and consumer, each index is only ever modified by one side. This eliminates the cost of having a shared locking mechanism.

We’ve introduced the first ring buffer implementation to Redox OS. Unlike Linux’s io_uring, the submission queue (SQ) and completion queue (CQ) are shared exclusively between userspace processes and are never accessed by the kernel.

is a new crate for ring buffer communication between userspace processes, also providing data structures for FFI use cases. It uses futexes as the main synchronization mechanism, with optional pipe file descriptor support.

Based on its FFI support, we’ve introduced the “redox-ring API” in relibc, inspired by Linux’s liburing.

liburing is a library for Linux’s io_uring, providing helpers for setting up and tearing down io_uring instances, as well as a simplified interface for submitting I/O requests.

Similarly, the redox-ring API allows applications to communicate with daemons that support ring buffers using custom protocols.

The API provides functions for managing ring buffers, shared memory, and requests.

  • redox_ring_queue_init_with_path() initializes a ring buffer connection to a daemon.
  • and allocate buffers from the shared memory pool.
  • obtains a submission queue entry (SQE) for preparing a request.
  • submits pending requests to the daemon.
  • waits for a completion queue entry (CQE), blocking if none is available.
  • marks a CQE as processed.

The API also provides functions for registering file descriptors, freeing allocated buffers, and tearing down ring buffer instances.

Memory Management and Shared Buffers

The implementation uses shared memory to exchange SQEs, CQEs, and I/O data between applications and daemons.

During initialization, the SQ, CQ, and data buffer pool are mapped into the application’s address space using the syscall with . This allows both sides to access the same memory without copying I/O data between processes.

The redox-ring API supports two buffer allocation strategies:

  • Fixed-size allocation: Uses a simple allocator that divides the shared memory pool into fixed-size chunks and maintains a list of available offsets.
  • Dynamic allocation: Uses the redox-buffer-pool crate to allocate buffers of varying sizes and alignments. The allocator uses B-trees to manage free and occupied memory regions.

Both allocation strategies return a pointer to the allocated buffer and its offset within the shared memory pool.

Once an operation has completed, the application can release its buffer, allowing the memory to be reused.

Session Creation and Management

The redox_ring_queue_init_with_path function opens the scheme ring handle and uses the system call on it to set up the ring buffer session with the given parameters. This returns file descriptors for the SQ, CQ, and shared buffer pool, which are mapped into the application’s address space. The application can then use the queues directly to submit requests and receive completions. On the scheme side, the worker task waits for entries in the SQ, processes them asynchronously and notifies the application on completion.

Example: Writing to RamFS

Ring buffer support was added to RamFS and NVMed. We also added tests that communicate with these storage daemons through the redox-ring API.

For example, writing data to RamFS involves the following steps:

  1. Open the target file and initialize a ring buffer instance to RamFS using redox_ring_queue_init_with_path().
  2. Register the file descriptor so that subsequent requests can reference it by index.
  3. Allocate a shared memory buffer and write the data into it.
  4. Obtain an SQE and specify the write operation, file index, buffer offset, data length, and file offset.
  5. Submit the prepared SQEs using . Multiple requests can be submitted in a single batch.
  6. Wait for CQEs, check the results, and release the buffers associated with completed requests.

Once all operations have completed, the application tears down the ring buffer connection.

We developed an async executor for device drivers, with a single interrupt vector and an SQ/CQ pair per core architecture. A single core is used at the moment, and multi-thread-per-core support is in progress. Furthermore, we updated NVMe driver to use the async executor, and more devices such as virtio are expected to follow.

With the executor, schemes that support Redox Rings can handle each I/O request in its own async task, with a worker thread spawned for each session between the application and the scheme. On teardown, the worker task is stopped, pending I/O operations are cancelled and shared resources are cleaned up.

Comparison between the and benchmarks, showing that is 14-15x faster. The benchmark performs I/O via synchronous system calls, while the benchmark uses the new Redox Ring interface.

Kernel and IPC optimizations

While it has substantially improved over the years, IPC is still quite slow on Redox, and this is important to optimize as ring buffers can only offset this overhead to a certain extent. This has been a focus of our work to improve system performance.

The test suite for Redox was expanded to include more targeted benchmarks that measure IPC latency, in particular acid ipc_latency_simultaneous, and also . Support was also added for repeating measurements and collecting more proper statistics (although still less feature-complete than e.g. ), making it easier to know whether changes in metrics are statistically significant and by how much.

Various single-digit speedups were attained from kernel refactors, such as eliminating redundant locking, hashmap lookups, and by adding a lower-overhead call for IPC, similar to seL4’s “reply-wait”.

Fast path switching without vector registers

Another source of overhead, from the flamegraphs, was found to be and , a few hundred cycles combined (tested on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X). These instructions save/restore vector registers, which is ~600 bytes on the CPU tested, and likely similar on other CPUs with AVX2 (which only userspace uses).

The optimization made here is that the kernel zeroes the vector registers if the caller and callee entered the kernel through syscalls, rather than saving/restoring (using , etc. as required for correctness).

Context switching can be triggered both by preemption, i.e. timer interrupts, and voluntarily from syscalls. After Redox destabilized its syscall ABI, instead preferring the symbols provided by , all syscalls will first go through a function call. Since the System V ABI clobbers all vector registers , it is almost zero-cost to also define Redox’s syscall ABI to do so. Luckily, the generated assembly code for was almost identical.

A major bottleneck during IPC is invoking the scheduler, as can be seen from various flamegraphs. The scheduler needs to access multiple data structures, primarily that takes up a large fraction of the overhead, and it also needs to acquire lots of locks, often blocking.

Direct context switching was implemented in kernel MR 694, resulting in a 15-20% IPC latency reduction. It separates the (reference) into the and the , where the former is the context owning the current timeslice, and the latter is the context whose registers/memory/file table is currently active. When direct switching has not occurred, these always coincide. Consequently, a client process calling a scheme (typically using our syscall) can completely bypass the scheduler and switch directly to the scheme, if ready, where the kernel will then prioritize returning to the the next time the scheme yields. This mimics the behavior of how complex syscalls are handled in monolithic kernels, and should also be more cache-efficient, among other efficiencies.

The kernel previously only supported 4k pages. This is still the case on non-x86, and for all userspace cases, but now the kernel physmap will be mapped as 2M when possible. TLB usage can thus theoretically be reduced by up to 512x for heavy CoW, and in practice, the highest obtained L1DTLB-miss rate from was -75%.

IPC roundtrip latency has been reduced from ~5800 cycles to ~2700 cycles, but this is still high compared to fast µkernels like seL4. Additional optimizations could be to reduce locking, and reduce the syscall entry overhead, but primarily to simplify the IPC primitive and remove possibly unnecessary parts such as request buffers. While not as applicable for nonlegacy applications, automatic page-borrowing of clients’ buffers (in ) is also a major source of overhead and in a benchmark similar to dd bs=4k if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null, the overhead is at least ~32k cycles per call. However, while the existing benchmarks are useful as an approximate lower bound on latency, more investigation will be required to determine the distribution of overheads for more realistic workloads, both with and without userspace ring buffers.

items.title: Reading and writing are less symmetric than you (probably) think
items.content:
I am talking about the I/O operations as used in computing here. A typical example of how this kind of thing is exposed are the POSIX syscalls and , which have the following C function prototypes:

ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);
ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count);

Now these are raw system calls; user programs use them directly, but they usually don’t. They normally go through some buffered IO layer; in the C standard library, this means and functions and , which split into a product of two values in a vestigial nod to record-based IO but are otherwise equivalent. For concreteness, suppose we’re interfacing with actual storage (i.e. not a pipe, socket, virtual filesystem etc.). Then conceptually, a “read”-class operation (like or ) grabs bytes from a file say on a disk somewhere and puts them into the specific memory buffer, and a “write”-class operation takes bytes in a memory buffer and writes them to the disk. Which definitely nice and symmetric—but there’s some important behavioral asymmetries between them, especially when errors are in the mix. The reasons have to do with buffering.

In general, file I/O operations in your program will not go directly to a storage device; data instead makes its way through several buffering layers (most of which can be disabled using various flags, but in normal usage these layers are on). These layers are there for good reason: on the kernel side, there’s what’s traditionally called the “buffer cache”. Storage devices are “block devices”, which means they store data in blocks. The block size depends on the device; on old hard disks it used to be 512 bytes, CDs, DVDs etc. tend to use 2k blocks, newer storage devices are now on 4k blocks. Block devices only read entire blocks at a time; that means random byte-aligned IO requests such as “read 100 bytes from disk at byte offset 1234567” or “write 2000 bytes to location 987654” can’t be directly passed to the device at all. The buffer cache is used to translate these requests into block-aligned read and write operations that the device understands; non-block-aligned writes also require reading the previous contents of the block that are not overwritten, and those go in the buffer cache as well. And of course, as the name suggests, it acts as a cache.

On the user-space side, we also have buffers, albeit for a different reason: and are system calls, and as such incur a transition to kernel space and back. They also need to check for and report errors every time they are invoked. And of course they actually need to do the work we want them to do – copy the data from () or to () the buffer cache. System call overhead varies between OSes, but it’s safe to assume that the whole process takes at least a couple hundred clock cycles in the best case. So for the overhead not to completely dominate the actual work being done, you generally want to be reading or writing at least a few kilobytes at a time. For scale reference, typical IO buffer sizes as of this writing are 4096 bytes (e.g. Visual C++ 2013 , Go /) or 8192 bytes (e.g. GNU libc , Java /).

Often there are more buffers too. For example, most hard drives and RAID controllers have their own caches, and it is not uncommon for user-space code to have several layers of buffering for various reasons. But this is enough to illustrate the basic structure.

All of these buffers are used in much the same way for reading and writing. So where’s the behavioral asymmetry between reading and writing that I’m talking about? You need to think about the state of the world (so to speak) after you call a -type call and how it differs from the state of the world after a -type call.

What happens when you issue an IO operation

Let’s look at what goes into servicing a -type call first: say you open a C and want to read the first 100 bytes via . The C standard I/O library notices that its buffers are currently empty, and tries to fill them up, issuing a system call to read say 4k worth of data. The kernel in turn asks the file system where the data for the first 4k of the file is located, checks the buffer cache to see if it already has a copy in memory, and if not, it issues a block read command to the storage device. Either way, the kernel makes sure to get those 4k of data into the buffer cache and from there copies them into the standard IO buffers in user-space memory, then returns. The standard IO library looks at the result of the system call, updates the state of its IO buffers, and then copies the 100 requested bytes into the memory buffer the app supplied.

And what if anything goes wrong? Say the file is smaller than 100 bytes, or there was an error reading from disk, or the file is on a network file system that’s currently inaccessible. Well, if that happens, we catch it too: if something goes wrong filling up the buffer cache, the kernel notices and returns an appropriate error to the I/O library, which can in turn pass errors on to the app. Either way, anything that can go wrong will go wrong the call returns. All the intervening layers need to do is make sure to keep the error information around so it can be passed to the app at the appropriate time.

Now let’s go the other way round: let’s open a fresh new file with a 4k write buffer and issue a 100-byte . This time, the IO library copies the 100 bytes from the app buffer to the write buffer… and immediately returns, reporting success. The underlying system call will not be executed until either the buffer fills up or is flushed as a result of calling , , or similar.

Quick imaginary show of hands: who reading this habitually checks return codes of or at all? Of those saying “yes”, who also remembers to check return codes of , or ? Probably not a lot. Well, if you don’t, you’re not checking whether your writes succeeded at all. And while these remarks are C-specific, this general pattern holds for buffered writer implementations. Buffered writing delays making the actual system call; that’s kind of the point. But it implies that error reporting is delayed too!

This type of problem is not restricted to user-space buffering either. The implementation of itself has similar issues: generally, after a successful call, your data made it to the buffer cache, but it hasn’t hit actual storage yet. The kernel will make its best effort to write that data to storage eventually (hopefully within the next few seconds), but if there’s a device error or a system crash, that data could still be lost. Both of these are relatively rare these days, so we don’t worry about them too much, right? Except for those of us who do.

Oh, and while will go to some lengths to make sure there are no nasty surprises when writing to local filesystems (for example, even with delayed write-back, you want to make sure to reserve free space on the disk early, lest you run out during write-back), at least on POSIX systems there can still be write errors that you only get notified about on , especially when network filesystems such as NFS or SMB/CIFS are in play (I’m not aware of any such late-reported error conditions on Windows, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t any). Something to be aware of: if you’re using these system calls and are not checking the return code of , you might be missing errors.

Which brings up another point: even on local file systems, you only have the guarantee that the data made it to the buffer cache. It hasn’t necessarily made it to the storage device yet! If you want that (for example, you’ve just finished writing some important data and want to make sure it actually made it all the way), you need to call on the file descriptor before you close it. The Windows equivalent is .

So, if you make sure to check error codes on every , and you before you (again checking errors), that means that once you’ve done all that, you’re safe and the data has successfully made it to permanent storage, right?

Well, two final wrinkles. First, RAID controllers and storage devices themselves have caches too. They’re supposed to have enough capacitors so that if the system suddenly loses power, they still have sufficient power to actually get your data written safely. Hopefully that’s actually true. Good luck. Second, the may have made it to storage, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s actually visible, because the metadata necessary to reach it might not have been written yet. Quoting the Linux man page on :

Calling does not necessarily ensure that the entry in the directory containing the file has also reached disk. For that an explicit on a file descriptor for the directory is also needed.

For better or for worse, I can’t recall ever seeing code doing this in the wild, though. I’m honestly not sure what the actual guarantees are that popular Linux file systems provide about these things. If you’re handling really important data, you should probably find out.

Buffering on the read side is great and pretty much transparent because if anything goes wrong, it will go wrong before you ever get to see the data, and you’ll get a proper error code.

Buffering on the write side is much trickier because it delays actual writing and error reporting in ways that most programmers are to be aware of, but usually aren’t. Few are aware of the actual steps necessary to ensure that data made it to storage safely, and some of the OS abstractions involved don’t exactly make things easier (see the quote above). Here be dragons.

Full buffering not line buffering mode, in case anyone’s feeling nit-picky. Actual block allocation—as in, selecting which physical location on the device file writes will end up—is often delayed in modern file systems, to make it easier to assign mostly-contiguous space to large files where possible. However, even with delayed allocation, you want to keep track of how much space is going to be available on the device once all currently pending writes complete, so that you can return “out of disk space” errors appropriately instead of discovering that you’re out of space 10 seconds after the user exited the app he was using to edit and save his Important Document. Because that would be bad. This sounds as though it’s just a matter of accounting, but it gets tricky with file systems that use extents and not bitmap-based block allocation: getting the last few discontinuous blocks on the device means that you might need extra space to store the file extents! All of which is to say: this stuff is tricky to get right. Yes, the name looks like it’s part of the C library buffered IO package, but it’s a proper syscall.

items.title: Simple circuits can create complex behaviors
items.content:
The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article.

All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors?

This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle.

In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors.

Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light.

The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses.

It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper.

By wiring the first to the second , we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit:

With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light.

If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss.

Over time, their paths look like this:

Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better…

Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn.

What if we give it another eye and flipper?

With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this:

Hmm… that didn’t work. Instead of steering towards the light, it steered from it!

If you didn’t know how their brains work, you might think that they light.

Why do they avoid the light? Well, if the light were to the spark’s left, then its left eye would sense more brightness, which means that its left flipper would wiggle faster, and this would cause it to turn right, away from the light. Conversely, if the light were to its right, then it would veer left.

But there’s a clever way to make this spark steer towards the light instead.

All we have to do is cross its connections. That is, we wire its left eye to its right flipper, and its right eye to its left flipper.

With this simple wiring change, it can finally steer towards the light.

But if you watch these sparks for a while, you’ll notice that there’s a problem.

While they can reach the light, they don’t slow down near it. Instead, they charge towards it like comets plunging towards the sun.

If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they’re the light.

Why do they attack the light? The problem lies in the of connection that we used.

To see why, we need to go back to our original spark. Remember how its flipper moved faster when the light got brighter? That’s because its eye and flipper were connected with an excitatory connection — where more input leads to more output.

If the light were a food source, then this spark would accelerate towards it, but it wouldn’t stop to enjoy its lunch.

Instead, we want the spark to slow down as it approaches the light. That is, we want its motion to be by light.

We can solve this by swapping out the excitatory connection for an inhibitory connection — one where more input leads to output.

With the original excitatory connection, the spark overshoots the light. With the inhibitory one, it slows down and gently comes to a stop.

Now let’s bring back the original two-eyed spark, but this time with inhibitory connections between its eyes and flippers.

Now, the flipper closer to the light moves slower, while the flipper on the opposite side moves faster, and this makes the spark turn towards the light.

Hooray! It can finally steer to the light and come to a stop. You can move the light in the graphic above (or the one below) to watch the sparks react.

They move as if they’re magnetically attracted to the light. If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they light.

We’ve now seen four very different behaviors, each achieved by making small changes to the neural circuitry of our virtual creatures.

If you saw creatures behaving like this in the wild, you might attribute some rudimentary intelligence to them.

But we’ve just shown you how this apparent intelligence arises from the bottom up, with just four neurons and two connections. There’s no magic here. In this view, behavior emerges from neural circuits.

And if a brain with just four neurons can do all this, imagine what your brain can achieve with nearly 100 billion neurons.

We can take this one step further.

In each of the simulations so far, the sparks all had identical brains. But biology is full of variation: No two brains are the same.

If we allow the connections between neurons to vary in strength, then each spark can react differently to the light.

They now have different preferences: The yellower sparks seem to love light more, while the redder sparks keep a cautious distance.

Just as a thermostat sets a preferred temperature, their brain wiring now determines their preference for light.

If you squint very hard at this, you might be able to see the rudiments of how brains encode preferences, such as a love for spicy food or an aversion to smelly cheese.

Of course, biology is far more complex than these simplified sparks. We intentionally gave them very simple brains, so that we can understand how every part works.

Their brains are also frozen in time. In reality, brains can learn: They alter their wiring to gain new skills such as learning to walk, ride a bicycle, or play a piano.

In the next article, we’ll watch this learning process in action, and see how these sparks rewire their brains to find the light.

items.title: Show HN: Marelleo, an open-source story box I built for my kids using ESP32
items.content:
It started as an irritation on holiday

Last summer, on holiday with friends and a small tribe of children, I came across the Toniebox. And honestly, I thought it was great. The child puts a figurine on the box, the story starts. They take it off, it stops. No screen, no menu, no parent to go and fetch. A two year old gets it in one second, which is roughly the highest level of usability anyone can reach.

The gesture is perfect. The business model, much less so. All these boxes work the same way: the object sells for a more or less reasonable price, and the money is made afterwards, on the content. Whether it’s the Lunii and its closed catalogue, the Yoto and its card packs, or the Toniebox and its figurines, every new story is a purchase, from a catalogue I don’t choose, on an object I don’t control. You’re not buying a player, you’re buying a subscription dressed up as a wooden toy. And that genuinely annoys me.

Meanwhile, I had been telling myself for years that I wanted to do electronics. Not as a dabbler: actually understand it. Except I knew nothing about it. I own a soldering iron that comes out every three years to reattach a headphone wire, never to build anything. The kind of guy who knows what a resistor is without ever having had to choose one.

The two urges met in the car on the way home. That would be my project. An RFID reader, a tag, a box that plays an audio track depending on what you put on it. Not to make a product. Just for my kids, and to learn.

The breadboard, or the right to get it wrong

I already knew what I didn’t want. A Raspberry Pi is a full computer just to play an MP3: too big, too hungry, and it takes twenty seconds to boot. A child putting a figurine down does not wait twenty seconds, they wander off and play. At the other end, the genuinely low level chips, the ones you program in C with a 400 page datasheet, are far too steep for a beginner who would like to hear a story that same evening.

While reading around, I came across the two things that made the project possible. First the : a microcontroller with WiFi built in, beefy enough to decode MP3, simple enough to program like an Arduino, and sold for a handful of euros. Then the , that perforated plate where you push components in without soldering anything.

It sounds like a detail. It is the whole project tipping over. On a breadboard, getting it wrong costs nothing: you unplug, you start again, nothing is damaged. When you’re learning, that is exactly the property you need.

So I read documentation, I talked it through with Claude, I drew wiring diagrams in a notebook. And very quickly, far too quickly to feel earned, I had a circuit that played an audio track when you put a tag on it. It was ugly, a plate of copper spaghetti, the speaker lying bare on the table. But it worked. A few hours, and I had a thing that told stories. I don’t think I had been that pleased with something made by my own hands since childhood.

The potentiometer, the smoke, and the smell of ski wax

What came next is less glorious. To set the volume I added a potentiometer, that little rotary knob which is nothing more than a variable resistor. Except that wired wrong, it no longer sets anything at all: it becomes a plain wire between plus and minus. That has a name, it’s called a short circuit, and it heats up terrifyingly fast.

It smoked. And it gave off a very particular smell, which took me a good while to place before it hit me all at once: . Burning wax. I recognise it instantly now, and it is never good news.

The battery was the other piece of work, and the one that made me think. You don’t connect a lithium cell to two wires and move on. You need a charge controller, a dedicated chip that decides when and how to fill it, that stops at the right moment and cuts out before anything stupid happens. You also need to fasten it down properly, because a lithium battery rattling around inside an enclosure and getting pinched is precisely the scenario in those videos nobody wants to watch.

And then a stupid detail: my battery’s connector did not match the one on the charging board. Two little white plugs that look alike, two different pitches, incompatible. So I did what you do at eleven at night on a Tuesday when you’re nearly there: I cut the connector off and soldered the battery straight on.

Immediate consequence, which I had not seen coming: no connector any more, therefore no way to unplug anything, and no switch anywhere in the circuit. The box was . Twenty four hours a day. A lithium cell hastily soldered into an object that never turns off, sitting in a child’s bedroom. Written down like that, it needs no comment.

That is the moment I stopped treating this lightly. Not out of fear, but because I understood that I was no longer tinkering with a gadget on the corner of a table: I was placing an electrical object into my children’s daily life. Everything else in the project follows from that realisation.

From breadboard to perfboard

The first consequence was leaving the breadboard, and it wasn’t only about safety.

A breadboard holds by friction. Every wire is held by a tiny spring, which is wonderful for trying things and disastrous for lasting. Move the circuit and a contact is lost, and the fault that follows is far worse than a clean failure: it is intermittent. You hunt a bug in your code for an hour and a half, you reread the same function twenty times, and it’s a wire that no longer touches.

The next step is : the same grid of holes, but on a printed circuit, with every component soldered in. You lose the right to be wrong, you gain a circuit that holds together. That’s where I really learned to solder, and above all where I understood that my repair soldering had nothing to do with manufacturing soldering. Repairing is remaking a joint that existed. Building is making a hundred in a row, all clean, all identical, knowing that the hundred and first is the one that will fail.

My kids unscrewed the knob until the wires tore off

For the enclosure I got very lucky: lent me his 3D printer and helped me through the first attempts. Without him I would still be cutting cardboard with a ruler. I drew my models in Fusion 360 on the free hobbyist licence, and printed.

The first version was too big and too fragile. And quality control arrived faster than expected, in the shape of three children aged 21 months, 5 and 7.

They broke the knob by turning it like animals. The volume knob ended up spinning with no end stop, round and round, and as it turned it wound the wires around themselves until it tore every one of them off. I opened the box onto a little nest of twisted copper. That’s where I learned the most important rule of the entire project: a five year old does not turn a knob, they unscrew it. And they don’t stop when it resists. They stop when it gives.

So I started over. I took every measurement again with callipers, component by component, so that each hole would land exactly where it should and each part would be held by plastic rather than by its wires. I thickened the walls, added pockets, lowered the height. Version after version, the object stopped looking like a prototype and started looking like an object.

Still in the spirit of nothing being allowed to give, I also abandoned self tapping screws. Screwing straight into printed plastic holds once, twice, and on the third go the material splits along the layers: the hole holds nothing any more and the part is fit for reprinting. The real answer is called a . You set it on the hole, come down on it with the tip of the soldering iron, the brass heats up, melts the plastic around itself and sinks in. As it cools you have a metal thread captured in the part, which you can screw and unscrew a hundred times.

And then came the only test that no technical argument passes on my behalf: Not politely: she put it on the living room shelf, among the objects you don’t tidy away when someone rings the doorbell. That also settles the cube shape, which I wasn’t sure about. An object for children that you don’t need to hide is an object that ends up being used.

In the opening photo, all of that is still visible: a circle engraved on the top, which says where to put the figurine because the antenna sits right underneath, the volume knob beside it, the play button, and the name raised in the front wall. The figurines are painted wooden people with an NFC sticker glued under their feet. Any object would do: a toy car, a token, a flat pebble. The child decides what tells what, and that is exactly what I wanted.

I wanted nothing left dangling

At that point I had a version that worked pretty well. But a wired circuit, however well soldered, is still a wired circuit. There is always a cable pulling on a joint, a module hanging off its legs, a connector that works loose when you shake it. And I had just spent a few weeks measuring, very empirically, how much my children shake things.

So I changed category and set about designing a . Everything that was scattered, brought together on a single board: the power supply, the charger, the amplifier, the SD card reader, the connectors. Every part in its place, nothing moving, nothing sticking out.

I used Claude to go from my wired circuit to a clean schematic, and that is where the division of labour became interesting. It reads a datasheet very well, spots that a pin needs a pull-up, works out a value, fetches a footprint from the library rather than copying it from memory. But it cannot route. Routing, that is to say physically drawing the path of every copper track between components without ever crossing another, is something I did by hand, in KiCad. Entire evenings spent moving lines by a tenth of a millimetre to squeeze a connection between two pads eight tenths apart.

That file has to be gone over with a magnifying glass before you send it, for a very concrete reason: you don’t order a single board. The minimum is five, manufactured and assembled in one go. One mistake in there isn’t a touch-up job, it is five boards for the bin and the whole invoice.

So I had it reread the entire schematic, line by line. It found three things I would never have seen, and each one would have cost the order.

The three mistakes caught before the order

The resistor that would have killed everything. To produce the 3.3 V the processor needs, I use a step-down converter, and I had put two resistors around it forming a divider. That is the normal way to set the output voltage. Except the chip I had picked comes in two families: an adjustable one, and a one. I had taken the fixed one. With my divider, the regulation would have read a voltage far lower than reality, concluded the output was too weak, and pushed. The arithmetic gives 13.7 V on a rail meant for 3.3. The WiFi module, the SD card, the NFC reader: all dead within a second of power-up.

The diode the wrong way round. In KiCad, pad number 1 of a diode is the cathode, and my file placed it the other way round. A reversed diode at that spot means the 5 V doesn’t come out, so the 3.3 V doesn’t exist, so the board doesn’t start at all. Five mute boards in one go, with no way of noticing without having them made.

And the checker that checked nothing. KiCad automatically verifies that tracks respect minimum clearances. Mine was configured with a minimum clearance of . It ran, it reported zero errors, and it approved absolutely anything, silently. That is the worst kind of bug: the tool that reassures you.

Once, the roles reversed and it gave me a silly amount of pleasure: was the one who spotted that two components in my bill of materials were out of stock, before it did. We turned that into a small program that queries the manufacturer’s catalogue and returns the stock and price of each part number, so that it never happens blind again. A part number is not a given: you recheck it on the day of the order, not the day before.

160 euros of boards, and nothing happens

I ordered from JLCPCB, who manufacture the board and populate it. For 160 euros I got five, already assembled, enough to keep one and give the rest to cousins and friends. Opening that parcel was one of the very good moments of the project. Green boards, crisp, components perfectly aligned, my name written on them, out of a file I had drawn on my sofa.

First contact with the manufactured object: I can’t plug the USB in. The factory had added a small strip of material under the socket, a breakaway tab used to hold the board during assembly, which you’re meant to snap off on arrival. I had to work up the nerve to break it by hand on a thirty euro board. That took me a good ten minutes of contemplation.

Then I plug it in and test. And nothing happens. The NFC reader’s LED blinks, but no figurine is recognised, nothing plays, nothing appears on the network. Nothing.

I spent a quarter of an hour telling myself I was an old fool who had just burned 160 euros on useless boards, and that it served me right. A genuinely bad moment. Then I went looking, methodically, unplugging the harnesses one by one.

The culprit came down to two wires. I had swapped the two middle conductors on the NFC reader’s ribbon, the ones carrying the serial link. That link always crosses over: what one transmits, the other has to listen to. Wired straight, both ends talk at the same time and nobody listens. The module powers up, its LED blinks away happily, and it never answers. It is the kind of fault that looks serious and is just carelessness.

And the best part comes last. I had fixed the cable, and it still didn’t work. For two stacked reasons: first, the program questions the reader , so until you restart, the repair is invisible. Second, the power switch cuts nothing at all while USB is plugged in, because it acts on the battery’s transistor and USB feeds the board by another path. So I was spending my time “restarting” a board that wasn’t restarting, to test a repair that was already done.

Cable finally unplugged and plugged back in, the long awaited line dropped onto the console:

bibliotheque : 4 figurine(s)

And for thirty seconds I thought it was still broken, because I couldn’t hear anything. The volume knob had been left at the bottom of its travel, at minimum. There is a poetic justice in ending a day of debugging on a volume problem.

But other than that: the board worked first time, with no rework at all. Not a single flying wire, not a track to scrape, not a resistor to replace. For a first board designed by someone who didn’t know what a footprint was three months earlier, I really did not expect that.

All that was left was to assemble everything into the enclosure, this time for good.

“Dad, we’ve already heard that one”

That remark is what set off the entire software side, and it brings us back to the starting point. A box with a frozen catalogue, even a catalogue of my own, becomes exactly the problem I wanted to avoid. The content had to belong to us, and it had to be able to change with no tool, no cable, and no me.

Everything goes through a web page, because there is no screen

The box serves its own page. You type its address into a browser, from a phone or a computer, and you see the figurines, the stories present on the SD card and what is playing right now. Nothing to install, nothing to update, no account.

For the very first start-up it opens its own WiFi network. A phone that connects to it brings up the setup page on its own, exactly like in a hotel: the box answers its own address to any domain name question, which makes the phone open the page without being asked. You pick your network from a list, type the password, it joins the house and closes its own network behind it.

The first version did that over Bluetooth. It worked, but it needed a dedicated app, which is untenable for an object you’d like to give away, and the Bluetooth stack weighed , nine per cent of everything the chip has, to be used exactly once in the life of the box. I threw it out without regret.

You send files from the page, they land on the SD card, you associate them with a figurine. A figurine carries as many tracks as you like, in whatever order you like, and they play through to the last one without looping. That opens everything up: recording your own voice to tell the kids a story when you’re away, putting on the songs they ask for on repeat, dropping in whatever you find online. MP3 and M4A, the two formats that come out of a phone or a Mac without converting anything.

One figurine, one URL, and it’s a radio

A track doesn’t have to be a file. You can give a figurine a , and the box connects to it and plays the stream as it arrives, storing nothing. It opens the connection, receives the audio in small pieces, decodes them and sends them to the amplifier while always keeping a few seconds in reserve, to absorb the network’s hiccups. If the connection drops it retries several times before giving up, because a home WiFi has its holes and a two year old should not have to understand why the music stopped.

So my children have radio stations that look like little wooden people, and I find that very satisfying.

And it updates itself over WiFi

This is the part I’m proudest of, because it solves a problem specific to finished objects. The box is screwed shut, assembled, sitting in the living room. If I want to fix something, I’m not going to take it apart every fortnight. So it fetches its new versions on its own.

It queries a fixed address, written into the program and deliberately impossible to change from the network. That is a security choice: a box that accepted being told where to look for its software would accept being made to install anything, and someone on the same WiFi would be enough.

If a newer version exists, a button appears in the page. It downloads it into a , the one that isn’t running, checks the fingerprint of the file it received, and only switches over if everything is intact. A power cut in the middle of a transfer therefore never leaves it mute: at worst it restarts on the old version, as if nothing had happened.

The safety net, and the time it would have been useless

That leaves the nightmare of a closed object: a version that starts correctly but whose networking is broken. It is valid, the box switches to it, and there is no longer any path to fix it. Hence a : a freshly installed version has to prove it can connect. Three start-ups without ever seeing the network, and the box goes back to the previous one by itself, before it even turns its radio on.

A version I had published was reopening its setup portal even though it knew the house network perfectly well: it was reading its saved credentials too early, before the radio had started, and concluding it had none. I had nothing to do. After three start-ups it went back to the previous version on its own, and I could repair it at my leisure.

Same family of mistake, funnier: each box opens a network carrying the last four digits of its hardware address, so that two boxes in the same house stay distinct. Except I was reading that address before the radio started, at which point it answers six zeros. Every box in the world would have been called Marelleo-0000.

And once, the net could have done nothing at all. My publishing script was only compiling one of the two hardware variants, the prototype. The printed board would have received the other one’s image: audio and SD card pinouts swapped, memory looked for on the wrong bus, and a header announcing 16 MB of memory on a chip that has 8. The worst part is that the trial period would not even have caught it, since the WiFi itself would have worked perfectly. It would have gone deaf and blind while believing itself in good health. We found that just before pressing the button.

One last anecdote, for anyone the detail amuses. One day the update started failing with no error message at all: the transfer would start, make progress, and the box would restart suddenly, in silence. Now, a silent failure says a lot. No error means the program had no time to write one, so it didn’t stop, it was interrupted. The download task had 8 KB of stack, and I had put a 4 KB buffer in it. There was nothing left for the encrypted handshake of the secure connection. The silence itself was the clue.

Three kids, three uses I hadn’t planned for

This is the best moment of the project, and it was in no specification. Each of them made the box their own, and none of the three ways is the one I had imagined.

Her music playlists on one figurine, her stories on another, and podcasts about insects. She chooses, she asks for additions, she runs her own catalogue.

Stories. Lots of stories, chained on a single figurine through to the last track, and replayed until I know them by heart.

Her lullabies, and her toddler podcasts live. Thank you France Inter and Radio Pomme d'Api.

One figurine, one gesture, and each of them has their own box inside the same box. That is exactly what I was after at the start, and it arrived through software rather than through a catalogue. The difference fits in one sentence: nobody sells me the content, and nobody can take it away from me.

I bought a 3D printer and built a workshop in the basement

There is one consequence I hadn’t foreseen, and it isn’t about the box.

I was starting to seriously abuse François’s kindness, since his printer had produced every one of my enclosures. And above all, I was enjoying all of this far too much: the evenings, the weekends, perfectly indefensible hours spent getting obsessive about a two millimetre fillet or the depth of a pocket. I decided this would not be my last electronics project, because I genuinely love it. So I bought a Bambu Lab A1.

I told myself it was a useful purchase: spare parts you stop rebuying, toys you repair instead of throwing away, custom storage. All of that is true. It wasn’t the reason.

And I installed it in the living room. A machine half a metre across, which blows, vibrates, runs for fourteen hours at a stretch and smells of hot plastic, in the middle of the room where Marceau is learning to walk. At the time it seemed perfectly reasonable. I was shown the door in no uncertain terms, and entirely deservedly: you do not install a production unit in a living room.

So I ran a network line over the mains down to the basement and set up a print station there. And it is frankly better than I imagined: I start a print from the sofa, it runs in the dark two floors below, and I go down to collect the part the next morning. No more noise and no more smell of hot plastic upstairs, and a living room that stays a living room. The fifth version of the enclosure came out of there. It’s the one in the opening photo.

The three enclosure parts to print, the board’s manufacturing files ready to drop into JLCPCB along with the bill of materials and component positions, the firmware source, and documentation that starts from zero: what to buy and for how much, what order to go about it in, the pinout of the module version, and the traps that cost me evenings. All MIT licensed, so do what you like with it.

You can start with the breadboard version, without soldering once, and only order the board if you catch the bug. That’s the path I took, and the one I’d recommend: the breadboard is the place where being wrong costs nothing.

And there are two ways to use it. Rebuild it as is, following the files, and get the same box my kids have. Or take it as a starting point: a different enclosure, a different speaker, different buttons, the code changed to your taste. Only one thing to know in that case, and it’s written in large letters in the repository: the firmware is written for that exact assembly, the pinout lives in the code, and a wire moved means a line to change. I flagged it because it is exactly the sort of detail that has you hunting a fault for an evening.

If you build one, I’d really like to see it.
